knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit only (wrinkled, yellow, fragrant). Unripe = bitter and nauseating.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet-tart pulp, eaten fresh. Leaves make a mild calming tea.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: wait for the fruit to fall or wrinkle fully. One vine can feed you for a week in season.

preparation: Eat only fully ripe (wrinkled yellow) fruit. Unripe fruit will punish you.
description: a vine with elaborate purple-and-white flowers and egg-sized green fruit that wrinkles yellow when ripe
lookalikeNote: The fringed purple-white flower is unmistakable. Only the wrinkled yellow fruit is food.
codex: The Southeast's passionfruit. Ugly flower, alien fruit, honest sugar.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: ripe wrinkled fruit — sweet-tart pulp
leaf tea, mild and calming

name: Wild Black Cherry

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild black cherry. Tall tree, hanging clusters of small dark fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit (dark purple-black). SPIT THE PITS — they contain cyanide compounds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet-tart fruit fresh or dried. Wilted leaves are dangerous to livestock.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick fully dark fruit; one tree can fill a pack. Dry cherries for winter.

preparation: Eat ripe fruit raw. Always spit the pits. Never chew them.
description: a tall tree with dark peeling bark and long hanging clusters of small dark cherries
lookalikeNote: Ripe = dark purple-black and sweet-tart. Red fruit isn't ready. Pits and wilted leaves are toxic.
codex: Cherry trees rain fruit in June. Eat the fruit, spit the pits — the rule is the recipe.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: ripe dark cherries — spit the pits
fallen fruit baits traps well

name: Serviceberry

knowledgeLevels.1: Serviceberry. White spring flowers, clusters of red-purple berries in June.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe berries (purple, soft). Seeds contain cyanide compounds like apple seeds — don't chew masses of them.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: blueberry-almond flavor, eaten fresh or dried. Early summer staple.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: June harvest; berries ripen unevenly — pick the dark ones, leave the red. Dry for winter stores.

preparation: Eat raw when fully purple. Don't chew large quantities of seeds.
description: a small tree with white starry flowers in spring and clusters of red-to-purple berries in early summer
lookalikeNote: Ripe = purple-black and soft. Don't gorge on the seeds (cyanide compounds, like apple seeds).
codex: June's gift. Tastes like blueberry met almond. The birds know the date before you do.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: sweet early-summer berries

name: Groundnut

knowledgeLevels.1: Groundnut. Twining vine in wet ground; dig for strings of round tubers.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the tubers. Cook well — raw causes stomach trouble. Exceptional protein.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: more protein than any tuber you know — the staple that fed whole villages.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: dig in fall along creek banks. Boil or roast thoroughly. Leave some tubers to regrow.

preparation: Dig tubers in fall. Cook thoroughly — never eat raw.
description: a twining vine in wet ground with brownish pea-flowers and strings of round tubers underground
lookalikeNote: Twining vine with compound leaves in wet soil = groundnut. Tubers grow in a string from the vine base.
codex: The Indian potato. Protein like a tuber shouldn't have. Cook it like you mean it.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: protein-rich tubers — cook thoroughly

name: American Ginseng

knowledgeLevels.1: Ginseng. Whorled compound leaves, red berry cluster. You've only read about this.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the slow-grown root. Harvesting wild roots is restricted in many states — it was poached near extinction.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: traditional adaptogen and tonic. The System notes it with interest; the forest keeps it rare.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: you don't forage this. You learn it, respect it, and leave it. The knowledge is the harvest.

preparation: Not foraged. Traditional use is dried root tea — in tiny amounts, from cultivated sources only.
description: a low woodland plant with a whorl of compound leaves and a small cluster of red berries — rare, and protected
lookalikeNote: Virginia creeper seedlings and young hickory sprouts fool beginners. Ginseng's leaf whorl is distinctive — and it isn't yours to dig.
codex: Worth more than gold, rarer than honesty. The forest keeps its ginseng; so do you.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: traditional tonic — cultivated only, never wild-harvested

name: Wild Ginger

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild ginger. Heart-shaped leaves flat on the forest floor. You've only read about this.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the rhizome smells exactly like ginger — but it isn't. Contains aristolochic acid: toxic to kidneys.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none safe in quantity. The System logged it as 'spice-adjacent, do not ingest'. Smell it, enjoy it, leave it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: knowing what NOT to eat is the highest level. The scent is the lesson.

preparation: Do not use as food. Historical spice use is discontinued for good reason (kidney toxicity).
description: low heart-shaped leaves hugging the forest floor, hiding small jug-shaped flowers at the base
lookalikeNote: Heart-shaped leaves with hidden jug flowers at the base. Gingery smell with NO culinary safety — leave it alone.
codex: Smells like ginger, acts like poison. The forest's reminder that smell is not a safety test.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: historical use only — aristolochic acid, toxic; do not ingest

name: Prickly Pear

knowledgeLevels.1: Prickly pear. Flat pads, sharp spines. The fruits are called tunas.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pads (nopal — vegetable), fruits (tuna — sweet). Burn off spines first or use tongs.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: pads are food AND water — chew for moisture. Fruits are high in sugar.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: singe spines over fire, then peel. Pads keep for days. In the desert, this plant is life.

preparation: Burn or scrape off glochids (tiny spines). Pads: grill or boil. Fruits: peel and eat.
description: flat paddle-shaped cactus pads, wicked spines, red-purple fruits
codex: Desert grocery store. Food, water, and medicine in one spiny package.

name: Mesquite

knowledgeLevels.1: Mesquite. Thorny tree, long bean pods. Desert staple.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pods (sweet, grindable into flour), wood (best firewood in the desert).
knowledgeLevels.3: Mesquite flour is protein-rich and sweet. Pods can be eaten raw when ripe.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest pods when dry and tan. Grind between stones. The wood burns hot and long — worth the thorns.

preparation: Pods: eat raw when ripe, or dry and grind into flour. Wood: best desert fuel.
description: thorny spreading tree, long tan bean pods, feathery leaves
codex: The desert's bread tree. Pods are candy and flour; wood is the finest fuel.

name: Salmonberry

knowledgeLevels.1: Salmonberry. Pink-orange berries, thorny canes. First berry of spring.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (eat fresh), young shoots (peel and eat like asparagus).
knowledgeLevels.3: They're watery — good for hydration, not calories. Eat by the handful while working.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: follow the salmonberry bloom — it marks the start of foraging season. Shoots are best before they leaf out.

preparation: Eat berries fresh. Peel young shoots and eat raw or steamed.
description: tall thorny canes, magenta flowers, salmon-colored raspberry-like berries
codex: Spring's first gift. Not calorie-dense, but they tell you the forest is waking up.

name: Huckleberry

knowledgeLevels.1: Huckleberry. Small dark berries, mountain slopes. Bears love them.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries only. Richer than blueberries, harder to find.
knowledgeLevels.3: Where huckleberries grow, bears feed. Pick noisily and in groups.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: they fruit heavily every 2-3 years. Remember the good patches — they're worth defending.

preparation: Eat fresh or dry for winter. Excellent dried.
description: low shrubs, small dark-purple berries, mountain slopes and clearings
codex: The mountain's candy. Worth the climb, worth watching for bears.

name: Yaupon Holly

knowledgeLevels.1: Yaupon holly. Evergreen shrub, red berries. The leaves make tea.
knowledgeLevels.2: It's the only native North American caffeine plant. Roast the leaves, steep like tea.
knowledgeLevels.3: The 'vomitoria' name is from ceremonial overuse — normal tea won't hurt you. Don't eat the berries.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: roast leaves dark for best flavor. This is coffee when there's no coffee. Trade-worthy.

preparation: Roast leaves in a pan until dark, then steep in hot water. Do NOT eat berries.
description: evergreen shrub, small red berries, oval leaves
codex: North America's only native caffeine. The bayou's coffee.

name: Saw Palmetto

knowledgeLevels.1: Saw palmetto. Fan palms with saw-tooth stems. Blue-black berries.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (edible, peppery-sweet), heart of palm (the growing tip — kills the plant).
knowledgeLevels.3: Berries are calorie-dense for their size. The saw teeth will cut you — harvest carefully.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: berries ripen in fall. Dry them for winter. Don't take the heart unless you're starving — it kills the plant.

preparation: Berries: eat raw or dried. Heart of palm: only in emergency (kills plant).
description: low fan palms, serrated stems, clusters of blue-black berries
codex: Florida's pantry palm. Berries feed you; the saw teeth remind you to be careful.

name: Sugar Maple

knowledgeLevels.1: Sugar maple. The sap makes syrup. Bark is grey, leaves turn brilliant in fall.
knowledgeLevels.2: Tap in late winter — when days thaw and nights freeze. Drill, spile, bucket.
knowledgeLevels.3: 40 gallons of sap = 1 gallon of syrup. Boil it down. It's work, but it's sugar.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: tap trees 10+ inches diameter, one tap each. The run lasts 4-6 weeks. Syrup keeps indefinitely.

preparation: Tap in late winter. Boil sap down 40:1 for syrup. Can also just drink the sap (slightly sweet water).
description: tall tree, grey bark, five-lobed leaves that flame orange in fall
codex: Liquid gold from a tree. The northeast's answer to sugar cane.
The forest's butter. Small nuts, big work — but they keep, and fat is fat.
description: a big many-stemmed shrub with round toothed leaves and nuts in ragged leafy cups

knowledgeLevels.1: Hazelnut. A big multi-stemmed shrub; nuts in leafy green cups.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the nut inside the cup and shell. Cup off, crack the shell. The cup's ragged leafy beak means European.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: rich in fat and protein — the forest's butter. Eat fresh or dried; they keep for months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: coppiced hazel stools fruit heaviest. Float-test (sinkers good). Weevils drill tiny holes — check. Roast lightly to wake the flavor.

lookalikeNote: The leafy cup with a ragged beak is unmistakable. Empty shells mean weevils got there first — float-test your harvest.
name: European Hazelnut
preparation: Husk the leafy cup, dry, crack. Roast briefly to improve flavor.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Corylus avellana

uses.note: sweet oily nuts — crack carefully, worth the trouble

codex: The oak's old bargain: tons of food, but you have to wash the bitter out first.
description: oval nuts in scaly cups, scattered under the big lobed-leaf trees

knowledgeLevels.1: Acorn. Oak nuts — bitter enough to warn you.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the nutmeat inside the shell. Shell, grind coarse, then leach: soak in several changes of water until the bitterness (tannin) is gone.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: leached acorn meal cooks into porridge or flatbread. A mast year feeds a village — the oaks drop tons.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: taste-test trees — some are far less bitter. Dry before storing or they mold. Leach cold (days) or hot (hours); never skip it.

lookalikeNote: Acorns are acorns — the danger isn't mistaken identity, it's skipping the leach. Bitter means tannin; tannin untreated means misery.
name: Pedunculate Oak Acorn
preparation: Shell, grind, leach tannins in repeated changes of water, then boil or bake. Never eat unleached in quantity.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Quercus robur

uses.note: leached acorn meal — porridge, flatbread

codex: Mast-year gold. The boars know; the jays know. Now you know.
description: tiny three-cornered nuts in spiny husks, under trees with smooth gray bark

knowledgeLevels.1: Beechnut. Small three-sided nuts in spiny little cases under the smooth gray-barked trees.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the triangular nutmeat. A few raw while gathering won't hurt you — but roast before eating in quantity (raw fagin upsets the stomach).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: rich oily nuts — roast like chestnuts, grind to flour, or press for oil. In mast years the ground is paved with them.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the spiny cases mostly hold empties — wildlife takes the filled ones first. Roast at a real heat; lukewarm doesn't finish the job.

lookalikeNote: The three-sided nut in a spiny case is unmistakable. The rule isn't identity — it's preparation: roast them.
name: Beechnut
preparation: Shell and ROAST before eating in quantity — raw fagin causes nausea. A taste raw while gathering is harmless.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Fagus sylvatica
German Federal Centre for Nutrition (bzfe) — Bucheckern guidance

uses.note: roasted nuts, flour, oil — always heat first

codex: The wild apple. Sour enough to wake the dead, sweet enough after frost to keep you alive.
description: small hard green-yellow apples on a low thorny tree

knowledgeLevels.1: Crab apple. Small hard apples on a thorny little tree.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the whole fruit — eat fresh (tart!), or cook down. The pips have a trace of cyanide compounds; don't make a meal of seeds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: cook into sauce or roast whole — heat tames the tartness. Dries well for winter.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: after the first frost they're sweeter. Old orchard trees and forest-edge thorn thickets both fruit.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable once you bite one — nothing else is that tart. Thorny tree + tiny apple = crab apple.
name: Crab Apple
preparation: Eat fresh or cook. Sweeter after frost. Don't chew the pips in quantity.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Malus sylvestris

uses.note: eat fresh tart, or cook/dry

codex: Summer in a berry. Your fingers will tell the story for days.
description: a low wiry shrub with dusty-blue berries that stain everything purple

knowledgeLevels.1: Bilberry. Low shrub, dusty-blue berries that stain your fingers purple.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the berries — eat fresh by the handful. The stain is the ID: bilberry juice is dark through and through.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the forest's summer sugar. Dries into raisin-like keeps. Leaves make a tea.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick with a berry comb in a good year and you'll fill buckets. They fruit best where the pines thin out.

lookalikeNote: Deadly nightshade berries can look like blueberries to a careless picker — but nightshade is a TALL plant with cherry-sized glossy berries in clusters and purple flowers. Bilberry is knee-high, berries single, juice dark. When in doubt, check the plant, not the berry.
name: Bilberry
preparation: Eat fresh or dry. The purple stain on your hands is normal — it's the anthocyanins.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Vaccinium myrtillus

uses.note: eat fresh, dry for winter

codex: Proof the forest likes you, occasionally.
description: tiny intensely fragrant red berries on low plants along sunny edges

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild strawberry. Tiny red berries, impossibly fragrant.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the berries. Smaller than garden ones, ten times the flavor. The smell gives them away before your eyes do.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: eat fresh — they don't keep and don't need to. A morale crop as much as a food.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: follow your nose along sunny trail edges in June. They hide under their own leaves.

lookalikeNote: Nothing poisonous mimics it closely — the fragrance is the guarantee. Mock strawberry (Potentilla indica) is bland and dry, not dangerous.
name: Woodland Strawberry
preparation: Eat fresh. They bruise if you look at them wrong.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Fragaria vesca

uses.note: eat fresh

codex: The hedgerow's pension plan: unglamorous, reliable, everywhere.
description: a thorny small tree with clusters of small red berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Hawthorn. A thorny shrub/small tree with clusters of small red berries.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the haws — mealy, mild, edible raw. Big seed inside; eat around it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: a steady fall food — not exciting, but everywhere. The old herbals call it a heart tonic (tea from leaves and flowers).
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: best after frost softens them. The thorns are the real harvest hazard — pick with care.

lookalikeNote: Single-seeded red haws on a thorny tree — distinctive. Don't confuse the thorns with blackthorn (sloes are blue-black and mouth-puckering).
name: Hawthorn
preparation: Eat raw around the seed, or cook into a sauce. Leaf/flower tea is the traditional heart tonic.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Crataegus monogyna

uses.note: haws raw or cooked
leaf/flower tea — traditional heart tonic

codex: Winter's vitamin C, hanging on a thorn.
description: bright red-orange oval fruits on arching thorny canes

knowledgeLevels.1: Rose hip. Bright red-orange oval fruits on the thorny rose canes.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the fleshy hip around the seeds. Eat the flesh — the seeds inside are covered in itching hairs. Or cook and strain.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: one of the richest wild sources of vitamin C — the scurvy answer when greens are gone. Tea, syrup, or dried.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest after frost when they soften. Dry whole for winter tea; the vitamin C mostly survives drying.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable on the cane — but never eat the hairy seeds raw; they itch going down and coming out. Strain them.
name: Dog Rose Hip
preparation: Eat the flesh raw avoiding the hairy seeds, or simmer and strain for tea/syrup. Best after frost.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Rosa canina

uses.note: flesh raw (avoid seeds), tea, syrup
vitamin C — the scurvy answer

codex: June smells of the flowers; September tastes of the syrup. Cook the berries — the bush insists.
description: a big shrub with flat plates of white flowers, later drooping clusters of black berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Elder. Big shrub; flat white flower plates in June, drooping black berry clusters in late summer.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe BLACK berries only — and cook them. Raw berries (and all green parts) can nauseate. The creamy flower heads make a fine tea/fritter cooked.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: cooked berries → syrup, sauce, wine. The classic cold-season remedy — elderberry syrup for winter coughs.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shake clusters into a bag; strip with a fork. Unripe green/red berries stay on the plant — only the black ones.

lookalikeNote: Ripe black clusters + flat flower-plate memory = elder. Red-berried elders are a different, harsher species — leave red clusters alone.
name: European Elder
preparation: COOK the ripe black berries — raw causes nausea. Flowers: tea or battered and fried.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Sambucus nigra

uses.note: cooked berries — syrup, sauce
elderberry syrup for coughs/colds

codex: Bear's garlic — the bears dig it first. The smell test never lies.
description: broad lily-like leaves carpeting damp spring woods, smelling of garlic

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild garlic. Broad green leaves carpeting damp woods in spring, smelling of garlic.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (and later the flower buds). The smell test is LAW: crush a leaf — real wild garlic smells strongly of garlic.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the spring tonic green — pesto, soups, wilted like spinach. The bulbs are edible too but leave them; the leaves are the crop.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest leaf-by-leaf, never whole patches. It carpets beech woods in April — where the beech is, the garlic follows.

lookalikeNote: DEADLY confusion possible: lily of the valley and autumn crocus leaves look nearly identical before flowering — but NEITHER smells of garlic. Crush and sniff every handful. No garlic smell = poison. This is the most important ID in the spring woods.
name: Wild Garlic
preparation: Eat raw or wilted/boiled. The garlic smell is the safety check — no smell, no eat.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Allium ursinum

uses.note: leaves raw/wilted — pesto, soup

codex: The king's spinach, outlasting the kings. It grows where people used to live — follow the ruins.
description: spinach-like plants with arrow-shaped dusty-coated leaves near old walls and yards

knowledgeLevels.1: Good King Henry. A spinach-like plant with arrow-shaped dusty leaves, often near old ruins and farmyards.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves and shoots — cook like spinach. The dusty white coating on young leaves is the ID mark.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the old cottage-garden spinach, gone wild. Boil to tame the oxalic edge; the water goes dark, the greens stay mild.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: perennial — the same plants return yearly. Cut young shoots like asparagus in early spring.

lookalikeNote: The dusty-white mealy coating on young leaves marks it. Older plants resemble orache — still edible, just tougher.
name: Good King Henry
preparation: Boil young leaves/shoots like spinach; discard the water. Eat young — old leaves get harsh.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Blitum bonus-henricus

uses.note: young leaves/shoots boiled like spinach

codex: The forest's lemon. Sour means vitamin C and a warning in the same bite.
description: arrow-shaped leaves with a sharp lemony tang

knowledgeLevels.1: Sorrel. Arrow-shaped leaves with a sharp lemon tang.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the leaves — chew one and the sourness is unmistakable. That tang is oxalic acid: fine as a flavoring, not as a staple.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: soup green (the classic sorrel soup), salad accent. A little goes a long way.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the arrowhead leaf with pointed basal lobes is the mark. Don't live on it — oxalic acid in bulk is hard on kidneys.

lookalikeNote: The lemon tang is the ID — nothing sour-tasting and arrow-leaved in these meadows will hurt you in normal amounts.
name: Common Sorrel
preparation: Eat sparingly raw; cook into soups. A flavoring green, not a bulk green.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Rumex acetosa

uses.note: leaves raw sparingly, soup green

codex: The Romans planted it as food and it never left. Neither should you, in April.
description: creeping patches of divided toothed leaves in shady damp spots

knowledgeLevels.1: Ground elder. Creeping patches of divided leaves in shady spots.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young spring leaves — the Romans ate it as a potherb. Older leaves get harsh; take the young unfolded ones.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: cook like spinach. Abundant enough to be a real bulk green in April and May.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the leaflets in threes with toothed edges, on grooved stems. It was a gout remedy once — hence podagraria.

lookalikeNote: Young leaves are safe and distinctive in threes. As with all umbel-family lookers, check the stem: ground elder stems are grooved, not purple-spotted (hemlock's mark).
name: Ground Elder
preparation: Boil young leaves like spinach. Take young unfolded leaves; old ones are harsh.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Aegopodium podagraria

uses.note: young leaves boiled like spinach

codex: The carrot's wild grandmother. The smell test is the difference between dinner and a funeral.
description: lacy white flower heads on tall stems; thin pale roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild carrot. Lacy white flower umbels; thin white roots.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: first-year roots (before it flowers). Scrape a root — real wild carrot smells of carrot. No carrot smell = don't dig.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: thin but real roots — soup material. The seeds are a sharp spice.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: first-year rosette only; second-year roots go woody. And the deadly rule: hemlock grows beside it — carrot smell or walk away.

lookalikeNote: POISON HEMLOCK is the deadly twin: hemlock has smooth purple-spotted stems and a foul mousy smell; wild carrot has hairy green stems and smells of carrot. Smell the root. When in doubt, walk away — hemlock kills.
name: Wild Carrot
preparation: Scrub and boil first-year roots. Confirm the carrot smell before eating.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Daucus carota

uses.note: first-year roots boiled — confirm carrot smell

codex: May's lace. Beautiful, edible — and the reason you learn hemlock before you learn lunch.
description: frothy white flower umbels on tall ridged stems along hedgerows

knowledgeLevels.1: Cow parsley. Frothy white umbels along every hedgerow in May.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves and shoots — mild, parsley-like. But this family demands respect: learn hemlock's marks first.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: a spring salad leaf in small amounts. Never the default green — the risk/reward only works when you're certain.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: ridged, slightly hairy green stems, NO purple spots, fresh green smell. Hemlock: smooth stem, purple spots, mousy stink. Know both cold.

lookalikeNote: Hemlock again: purple-spotted smooth stems + foul smell = death. Cow parsley: ridged hairy green stems, no spots, fresh smell. If you can't tell them apart yet, don't pick either.
name: Cow Parsley
preparation: Young leaves raw in small amounts or wilted. Only when hemlock's marks are memorized.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Anthriscus sylvestris

uses.note: young leaves — only with hemlock ID certain

codex: Gold in the moss. The apricot smell is the signature — learn it once, eat for life.
description: golden funnel-shaped mushrooms with an apricot smell, in mossy woods

knowledgeLevels.1: Chanterelle. Golden funnel-shaped mushrooms smelling faintly of apricots.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the whole mushroom — but ALWAYS cook wild mushrooms. The false chanterelle has true thin gills; real chanterelles have blunt forked ridges, not gills.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the prized one — sauté in fat. They fruit in the same mossy spots year after year; remember the spot.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: ridges not gills, apricot smell, flesh white inside. Cut, don't pull — the mycelium fruits again.

lookalikeNote: False chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca): true thin gills, darker orange, no apricot smell — not deadly but a bad meal. Real ones have blunt ridges, not gills.
name: Chanterelle
preparation: ALWAYS cook wild mushrooms. Sauté; never eat raw.

uses.note: sautéed — always cooked

codex: Steinpilz. The mushroom that built foraging cultures — dry them and winter gets easier.
description: big brown-capped mushrooms with thick pale stems and sponge pores, no gills

knowledgeLevels.1: Porcini. Big brown-capped boletes with thick pale stems, under spruce and beech.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: cap and stem — cook always. Check the pores: white-to-olive sponge, no gills. Nibble-and-spit a crumb: bitter = the inedible bitter bolete.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the king of mushrooms — fresh sautéed or dried (they dry superbly and keep all winter).
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: white net-like pattern on the upper stem marks true porcini. Slice stems lengthwise — maggots show as tunnels; share with no one.

lookalikeNote: Bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus) looks alike but isn't poisonous — just vile. Nibble and spit: bitter = toss it. No gilled mushroom is a bolete.
name: Porcini
preparation: ALWAYS cook. Dry surplus — dried porcini are winter gold.

uses.note: sautéed fresh or dried — always cooked

codex: A soccer ball you can eat — if it's white all the way through. The cut test is non-negotiable.
description: a huge smooth white ball sitting on the ground, sometimes head-sized

knowledgeLevels.1: Giant puffball. A huge white ball on the ground — sometimes the size of your head.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the whole ball, sliced like bread and fried — BUT only if pure white inside. Cut top to bottom: any hint of a cap-and-stem shape inside means a deadly Amanita button. Walk away.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: mild, filling — fry slices like tofu steaks. One ball feeds several people.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pure white and marshmallow-firm = good. Any yellowing = too old (stomach trouble). Small round whites are the dangerous ones to confuse — only take the giants you're sure of.

lookalikeNote: Young death caps and destroying angels look like small white balls before they open. The rule: cut top to bottom — pure white and featureless throughout, or it isn't food. Any shadow of gills, cap, or stem = deadly.
name: Giant Puffball
preparation: Slice and fry. ONLY when uniformly pure white inside — cut every specimen top to bottom first.
sources: Missouri Dept. of Conservation — giant puffball field guide

uses.note: fried slices — only pure-white specimens

codex: Beautiful, fragrant, lethal. The reason the smell test exists.
description: broad paired leaves with sweet white bell flowers in spring, red berries later

knowledgeLevels.1: Lily of the valley. Sweet white bell flowers in spring; broad leaves otherwise.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Cardiac glycosides — every part, especially the red berries. The leaves are the wild-garlic killer: identical-looking, no garlic smell.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none as food. Know it so you don't eat it by mistake.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: two broad leaves per stem, no garlic smell when crushed. Teach everyone the smell test.

lookalikeNote: The wild-garlic twin that kills: same broad leaves, same woods, same season — but crush it and there's NO garlic smell. Smell every leaf.
name: Lily of the Valley
preparation: DO NOT EAT. All parts toxic.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Convallaria majalis

codex: It flowers without leaves and leafs without flowers — and punishes the careless in both seasons.
description: broad fleshy leaves in spring (no flowers), purple crocus flowers in fall (no leaves)

knowledgeLevels.1: Autumn crocus. Purple crocus-like flowers in fall with NO leaves; broad leaves in spring with no flowers.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Colchicine — a few grams can kill. The spring leaves are the second wild-garlic killer: broad, green, garlic-smell-free.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none as food. A medicine plant for specialists only — not you, not now.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: leaves emerge from a bulb-like corm with no stem; wild garlic leaves have distinct stems. When in doubt, smell.

lookalikeNote: Meadow saffron's spring leaves mimic wild garlic — thicker, fleshier, stemless, and smelling of nothing. The garlic smell test catches it.
name: Autumn Crocus
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Colchicine poisoning is slow and irreversible.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Colchicum autumnale

codex: The one that ends foragers. Half a cap, no second chances. Respect is survival.
description: an olive-green capped mushroom with white gills, a skirt-like ring, and a sac at the stem base

knowledgeLevels.1: Death cap. An olive-green capped mushroom with white gills, a ring on the stem, and a cup at the base.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Amatoxins — half a cap can kill an adult. It tastes fine; that's the horror. The young 'buttons' look like small white balls.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. Learn it to avoid it — and to warn others.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: greenish cap + white gills + stem ring + basal cup (volva) = walk away. Dig up the base to check for the cup; the cup is the signature.

lookalikeNote: Kills more foragers than any other mushroom. Buttons mimic puffballs and field mushrooms — always excavate the base: the volva sac gives it away.
name: Death Cap
preparation: DO NOT EAT. There is no safe preparation.

codex: The mushroom every child draws and no forager eats.
description: the classic red-and-white-spotted toadstool

knowledgeLevels.1: Fly agaric. The storybook mushroom — bright red cap with white warts.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Ibotenic acid — toxic and deliriant, not usually deadly but never food. The white warts wash off in rain, so don't trust a 'plain red' ID.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none as food. The fairy-tale look is the warning — nature's red flag.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: same family as the death cap — white gills, stem ring, basal cup. If it has the amanita architecture, it isn't dinner.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable when fresh — but rain washes the white warts off, leaving a plain red cap. Check the stem base for the amanita cup regardless.
name: Fly Agaric
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Toxic and psychoactive — not food by any preparation you should attempt.

codex: Belladonna — the beautiful lady with a body count. Sweet berries, bitter end.
description: a tall plant with dull purple bell flowers and shiny black cherry-sized berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Deadly nightshade. A tall plant with purple bell flowers and shiny black cherry-like berries.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Atropine — a few berries can kill. Sweet-tasting, which is why children die of it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none as food. The berries can look like big bilberries to the careless — check the plant: nightshade is waist-high with purple bells.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: solitary shiny berries in leaf axils, purple-brown bells. Teach children on sight — this one kills the young first.

lookalikeNote: The bilberry confusion kills: nightshade berries are cherry-sized, glossy, on a TALL plant with purple bell flowers. Bilberries are pea-sized on a knee-high shrub. Size and height tell them apart.
name: Deadly Nightshade
preparation: DO NOT EAT. A few berries are a lethal dose.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Atropa belladonna

codex: What killed Socrates grows by the creek. Purple spots, smooth stem — learn it like your life depends on it.
description: tall white flower umbels on smooth purple-blotched stems, smelling faintly foul

knowledgeLevels.1: Poison hemlock. Tall white umbels on smooth stems blotched purple.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Coniine — Socrates' cup. Every part kills; the roots are the worst. The purple-spotted smooth stem is the mark.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. Learn it because everything you want to eat has a cousin that looks like this.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: smooth hollow stem + purple blotches + foul mousy smell when crushed = hemlock, always. Wild carrot: hairy green stem, carrot smell. Cow parsley: ridged hairy stem, no spots.

lookalikeNote: The killer all edible umbels are measured against. Purple spots + smooth stem + mousy stink = death. Memorize it before you pick a single wild carrot.
name: Poison Hemlock
preparation: DO NOT EAT. No safe part, no safe preparation.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Conium maculatum

codex: The forest's spring water — sweet, free, and gone by May. Take little, thank the tree.
description: white-barked birch trunks weeping sweet sap in early spring

knowledgeLevels.1: Birch sap. In early spring the white-barked birches run sweet — tap a trunk and it weeps.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the spring sap — a thin sweet drink, faintly mineral. Tap high-side, small hole, and never take much from one tree.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: drink fresh as a spring tonic; boil down to syrup (it takes a LOT of sap). The year's first sweet thing.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: tap when nights freeze and days thaw — the run lasts weeks. Plug the hole with a twig after; the tree gave you a gift, don't wound it.

lookalikeNote: White peeling bark + drooping twigs = silver birch. Tap birches, not beeches — and only in the spring run.
name: Birch Sap
preparation: Drink fresh or boil to syrup. Tap modestly; plug the tap hole.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Betula pendula

uses.note: drink fresh, boil to syrup

codex: The Amazon's staple root. Sweet varieties carry under 50 mg/kg cyanide — peeling and thorough cooking clears it. Feeds half the tropics for a reason.
description: tall stalks with hand-shaped leaves and thick pale roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Manioc. Tall stalks, hand-shaped leaves, thick roots.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: roots (the food — peel first), young leaves (cooked greens only, never raw). Rot fast after harvest.
knowledgeLevels.3: Sweet varieties: peel + cook through and they're safe. Bitter varieties can carry 400 mg/kg cyanide and need days of work — grate, ferment 2-3 days, press out the juice, roast into farinha. Cooking alone does NOT clear bitter roots (boiling removes only 10-75%).
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: bitter roots yield more starch and make the best farinha — if you do the full detox. Sweet for quick meals, bitter for the pantry. Harvest only what you'll process within days.

lookalikeNote: Sweet and bitter varieties look IDENTICAL — same palmate leaves, same roots. The only safe test is knowledge: know the field it came from, or the person who planted it. If you don't know which it is, treat it as bitter.
name: Sweet Manioc
preparation: Peel completely (toxins concentrate in the peel), then boil, roast, or fry until fully cooked through. Never eat raw. Roots rot within days of harvest — cook or process fast.
sources: FAO CXC 73-2013 (Codex code of practice for cassava processing)

uses.note: roots peeled and cooked; young leaves boiled
farinha (toasted flour) from fully detoxed roots

codex: The dangerous twin. Bitter manioc feeds millions — but only because the processing is a ritual nobody skips. Grate, ferment, press, roast. In that order, every time.
description: tall stalks with hand-shaped leaves and thick pale roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Manioc. Looks exactly like the sweet kind. That is the problem.
knowledgeLevels.2: The cyanide lives in linamarin, locked in the root. Grating ruptures the cells so the enzyme linamarase can break it down — that's why you grate BEFORE fermenting.
knowledgeLevels.3: The full rite: peel, grate, ferment the mash 2-3 days (never less), press out every drop of juice, roast dry. Fermenting less than 2 days leaves dangerous cyanide in the flour.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the poison is the point — bitter varieties out-yield sweet and their farinha keeps for months. Sulfur-rich foods (meat, eggs) help your body clear small doses. Never let the desperate eat it half-processed.

lookalikeNote: Indistinguishable from sweet manioc by sight — same leaves, same roots. Bitter roots can carry up to 400 mg HCN per kg (8x sweet). This is the one that kills when hunger makes people shortcut the work.
name: Bitter Manioc
preparation: Cooking alone is NOT enough — boiling removes only 10-75% of the cyanide. Full detox: peel, grate to rupture the tissue, ferment the mash 2-3 days, press out ALL the juice, then roast dry into farinha or gari. Skip a step and it can kill (~200 deaths a year worldwide).
sources: FAO CXC 73-2013 (Codex code of practice for cassava processing)

uses.note: only after the full grate-ferment-press-roast detox
tucupi (the pressed juice) is lethal raw, a delicacy after days of boiling

codex: The floodplain palm. Fatty purple pulp, eaten by the bowlful with farinha. Açaí feeds the river towns — and climbing the palm is the price.
description: a slender palm with a crown of arching fronds and hanging clusters of dark purple berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Açaí. Dark berries on a tall thin palm.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (mash for pulp). The trunk's heart (palmito) is food too — but cutting it kills the palm.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the pulp is fatty and filling, a real meal with farinha. Spoils in a day — eat it fresh or not at all.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: multi-stemmed clumps regrow after cutting — harvest palmito from the suckers, never the mother stem. Best pulp comes from berries soaked warm, not hot.

lookalikeNote: Bacaba and patauá are close cousins with similar berries — all three are safe. The dangerous lookalike is none: learn the palm, not the berry.
name: Açaí
preparation: Soak the berries in warm water, then mash and strain — the thick purple pulp is the food. Eat fresh; it ferments within a day.

uses.note: berry pulp mashed and strained
heart of palm from sucker stems (sustainable cut)

codex: The forest's savings account. One pod holds a dozen nuts, each one pure fat and protein. The trees only fruit in old-growth — no plantation has ever matched the wild.
description: a giant emergent tree dropping heavy cannonball pods the size of a head

knowledgeLevels.1: Brazil nut. Huge tree, huge pods, rich nuts.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: nuts (eat). The pod is a wooden cannonball — crack it, don't bite it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: among the most calorie-dense wild foods on earth. A handful is a meal. Keep dry and they last months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: agoutis bury the nuts and forget some — that's how the tree plants itself. Watch where agoutis feed and you'll find the mother trees.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else drops pods like cannonballs. The agouti is the only animal strong-toothed enough to open them — follow the agouti.
name: Brazil Nuts
preparation: Crack the woody pod (machete, rock, or patience), extract the nuts, eat raw or roasted. Don't stand under the tree in pod season.
sources: FAO non-wood forest products: Brazil nut

uses.note: nuts raw or roasted, in the shell they keep for months

codex: Not a tree — the world's biggest herb. An old roça always has banana: the first thing planted, the last thing to die.
description: a giant herb with huge paddle leaves and hanging hands of curved yellow-green fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Banana. Peel, eat.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (ripe raw, green cooked), flower bud (cooked), stalk core (cooked).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: instant energy, potassium. The leaves wrap food for roasting and thatch a roof.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the 'tree' dies after fruiting — the suckers at its base are the next crop. Cut the old stem to feed the young.

lookalikeNote: Plantains look identical on the plant — they're starchier and must be cooked. Taste a corner: sweet means banana, bland means plantain.
name: Banana
preparation: Peel and eat ripe. Green ones cook like a vegetable. The flower bud and inner stalk are cooked greens.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw; green fruit cooked
flower bud and stalk core, cooked

codex: The smell gives it away before your eyes do — chocolate and pineapple at once. The pulp is dessert; the seeds are chocolate waiting to happen.
description: a small tree with huge brown fuzzy pods hanging from the trunk, smelling of chocolate and pineapple

knowledgeLevels.1: Cupuaçu. Big brown pod, incredible smell, tangy cream inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat raw), seeds (dry and grind for cupulate chocolate).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the pulp is rich and filling — juice it, or eat it straight. High in fats that feed you fast.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruits drop when ripe — gather from the ground, don't pick. The pulp ferments fast; eat or juice within a day.

lookalikeNote: Cacao's big cousin — both fruit straight from the trunk (cauliflory). Cupuaçu pods are bigger, brown and fuzzy; cacao pods are smaller, ribbed, yellow-red.
name: Cupuaçu
preparation: Crack the pod, scoop the creamy pulp raw. Seeds can be dried and ground like cacao — that's cupulate, the Amazon's chocolate.

uses.note: pulp raw
seeds dried and ground as chocolate (cupulate)

codex: Chocolate grows on trees here — almost. The pulp is the treat; the seeds are a week of work away from chocolate.
description: an understory tree with ribbed yellow-red pods growing straight out of the trunk

knowledgeLevels.1: Cacao. Sweet pulp around bitter seeds, straight off the trunk.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat fresh), seeds (ferment, dry, roast for chocolate).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: pulp is quick sugar and water. The seeds are fat and calories — but only after fermenting 3-5 days and drying.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: unfermented seeds are just bitter. The fermentation is the whole trick — heap them in leaves, turn daily, then dry in the sun.

lookalikeNote: Cupuaçu's smaller cousin — same trunk-fruiting habit. Cacao pods are ribbed and colorful; cupuaçu pods are brown and fuzzy.
name: Cacao
preparation: Split the pod and suck the sweet-tart pulp off the seeds — eat it fresh. The seeds themselves are bitter raw; they need fermenting and drying to become chocolate.

uses.note: pulp sucked fresh off the seeds
seeds fermented, dried, roasted — chocolate

codex: The Amazon's breadfruit — starchy, nutty, filling. And the one palm you can harvest the heart from guilt-free: it suckers, so the clump lives on.
description: a clustering spiny palm hung with bunches of orange-red plum-sized fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Pupunha. Orange fruit clusters on a spiny palm.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (boiled), heart of palm (the sustainable one — cut one stem, the clump regrows).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the boiled fruit eats like a chestnut crossed with squash — real starch, real meal.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: watch for the weevil grubs in fallen fruit — the locals eat those too. Cut heart-of-palm only from multi-stem clumps.

lookalikeNote: The spiny trunk is the ID — rings of black spines. Tucumã is spiny too but its fruit is smaller and oilier.
name: Pupunha (Peach Palm)
preparation: Boil the fruit in salted water 30-60 minutes until the flesh softens — eating it raw is gritty and unpleasant. Split, remove the seed, eat the starchy flesh.

uses.note: fruit boiled in salted water
heart of palm from sucker stems

codex: The weed-tree that feeds everyone. Guava colonizes every clearing — where people were, guava still is.
description: a shrubby tree with smooth peeling bark and round yellow-green fragrant fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Guava. Fragrant, soft, pink inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat whole). Leaves make a tea for gut trouble.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: vitamin C by the handful. The leaf tea is a real antidiarrheal — worth knowing.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: guava marks old habitation — a guava thicket means a roça was here, and roças mean manioc gone wild nearby.

lookalikeNote: The peeling bark is the giveaway — smooth, mottled, like sunburn peeling. Nothing poisonous in the Amazon looks like this.
name: Guava
preparation: Eat ripe and soft, skin and all. Hard green ones need ripening off the tree — or cooking.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw, whole
leaf tea for diarrhea

codex: Born in South America, raised by the whole tropics. The crown you twist off is the next plant — stick it in the ground.
description: a spiky rosette of sword leaves with a single golden cone of a fruit rising from the center

knowledgeLevels.1: Pineapple. Spiky outside, gold inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat ripe). The crown replants.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sugar, water, and bromelain — the enzyme that tenderizes meat and burns your tongue if you overdo it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: plant the crowns in a row and you have a living fence that fruits. Unripe juice tenderizes tough meat in an hour.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else makes this fruit. Unripe it is all acid — the mouth-burn is the warning, not poison.
name: Pineapple
preparation: Twist off the crown, slice away the spiky skin, eat. Unripe pineapple burns the mouth — wait for gold and fragrance.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw
unripe juice as meat tenderizer

codex: The vine that smells like the tropics are supposed to. Tart, fragrant, and the juice knocks you pleasantly sideways at dusk.
description: a climbing vine with alien-looking purple-and-white flowers and wrinkled purple-yellow fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Maracujá. Wrinkled fruit, incredible smell, scoop the inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp with seeds (eat). The wrinkled ones are the sweet ones.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the juice is mildly sedative — the old-timers drink it at night for sleep.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the vine fruits heaviest on forest edges where it climbs into the light. Follow the smell in fruiting season.

lookalikeNote: Many passionflower vines are ornamental with inedible fruit. Edulis has the wrinkled purple fruit and three-lobed leaves — when in doubt, smell: ripe maracujá is unmistakable.
name: Maracujá (Passion Fruit)
preparation: Cut and scoop the aromatic pulp — seeds and all. Wrinkled skin means ripe and sweet.

uses.note: pulp scooped raw
juice as a mild sedative

codex: The vitamin bomb. Sixty times the vitamin C of an orange — the floodplain's answer to scurvy, if you can stand the sour.
description: a bushy riverside shrub with small round red-purple fruit, standing in the floodwater half the year

knowledgeLevels.1: Camu-camu. Sour little riverbank fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat fresh, juice it).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the richest natural vitamin C source known. Eat a handful a week and scurvy can't touch you.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it fruits as the waters rise — the flood brings the medicine. Pulp freezes and dries well for the dry months.

lookalikeNote: Grows where the river stands — the flood tolerance is the ID. Small myrtle-family fruit, nothing toxic mimics it here.
name: Camu-camu
preparation: Eat the tart fruit fresh or squeeze for juice — staggeringly sour, staggeringly full of vitamin C. A spoonful of pulp covers days of need.

uses.note: fruit fresh or juiced
vitamin C — scurvy prevention

codex: The custard apple of the Amazon. Fragile, perfumed, and gone in a day — eat it standing under the tree.
description: a small tree with spiny green heart-shaped fruit that turns yellow and perfumed when ripe

knowledgeLevels.1: Soursop. Spiny green fruit, white creamy inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat — SPIT OUT the seeds). Leaves make a strong tea.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the pulp is rich and filling. The seeds carry annonacin — swallow one whole and you're fine; chew them and you're not.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: don't make soursop a daily staple — heavy long-term use of the pulp and leaf tea is linked to nerve trouble. A treat, not a diet.

lookalikeNote: Biriba is the lookalike — same family, softer spines, smaller fruit. Both are safe; both hide seeds you shouldn't chew.
name: Soursop
preparation: Open ripe fruit and eat the pulp, spitting out the large black seeds — they are toxic (annonacin). Never chew or grind the seeds.

uses.note: pulp raw, seeds spat out whole
leaf tea — strong, use sparingly

codex: Soursop's gentler cousin. Custard in a spiny jacket — the Amazon's ice cream before freezers.
description: a small tree with yellow heart-shaped fruit covered in soft fleshy spines

knowledgeLevels.1: Biriba. Yellow spiny fruit, custard inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat). Skin and seeds are not food.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet, soft, fast energy. Ripe means yellow and fragrant — green means wait.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruits bruise if you look at them wrong. Eat under the tree; carry pulp, not fruit.

lookalikeNote: Soursop's lookalike — smaller, yellower, softer spines. Safe either way, so the confusion costs you nothing but a name.
name: Biriba
preparation: Eat fully ripe (yellow, fragrant) — scoop the custard pulp. Unripe fruit is bland and chalky.

uses.note: ripe pulp raw

codex: Patience fruit. Pick it yellow or pick it twice — the unripe latex will glue your mouth shut and you'll deserve it.
description: a tall tree with round yellow fruit that drips sticky white latex when unripe

knowledgeLevels.1: Abiu. Round yellow fruit, sweet jelly inside.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat when fully ripe). Unripe fruit is full of sticky latex — avoid.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: translucent sweet pulp, eaten with a spoon. Good quick calories.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: grease your lips before eating — even ripe fruit leaks a little latex. Fully tree-ripened is the only kind worth picking.

lookalikeNote: Unripe abiu looks ready but isn't — the latex is the test. If white sap beads from the stem, walk away and come back in a week.
name: Abiu
preparation: Eat only fully ripe (deep yellow, slightly soft) — scoop the translucent pulp. Unripe fruit's latex sticks lips together painfully.

uses.note: ripe pulp scooped raw

codex: The spiny one. Tucumã doesn't want to be picked — the trunk is armored. The orange pulp is worth the negotiation.
description: a tall spiny palm with dense bunches of small orange oily fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Tucumã. Orange palm fruit, spiny trunk — approach carefully.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat), seed (hard, not food). The spines are the tax.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: oily, vitamin-A-rich pulp. Real food, and the fiber from the leaves makes hammocks.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cut the whole bunch with a long pole — never climb a spiny palm. Fallen fruit ferments fast; gather daily.

lookalikeNote: Spiny trunk + small orange fruit = tucumã. Murumuru is spiny too but shorter, with bigger fruit. Both are safe.
name: Tucumã
preparation: Eat the oily orange pulp fresh off the seed. The trunk spines are vicious — harvest bunches with a pole, never by climbing.

uses.note: oily pulp fresh

codex: Açaí's quiet cousin. The bacaba wine — purple, oily, faintly sweet — is what the river towns drink when açaí runs thin.
description: a tall slender palm with hanging clusters of dark purple oily berries, thinner than açaí

knowledgeLevels.1: Bacaba. Dark berries like açaí, oilier.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (mash for drink).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the 'wine' is thinner and oilier than açaí — an acquired taste that grows on you fast when hungry.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruits when açaí doesn't — the two palms stagger their seasons. Learn both and the river never runs dry of purple.

lookalikeNote: Açaí vs bacaba: açaí berries are rounder and the palm clumps; bacaba is single-stemmed and taller. Both safe — the confusion is harmless.
name: Bacaba
preparation: Soak berries warm, mash and strain like açaí — the result is an oily purple drink. Eat fresh.

uses.note: berry drink mashed and strained

codex: The olive tree of the Amazon. The fruit is nearly half oil — press it and you have cooking fat that doesn't spoil.
description: a very tall palm with long clusters of green-purple fruit that feels greasy to the touch

knowledgeLevels.1: Patauá. Tall palm, greasy-feeling fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit pulp (eat, press for oil).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the oil is the prize — cooking fat that keeps without refrigeration. The pulp itself is rich and filling.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: mash the pulp in warm water and the oil floats — skim it. A bottle of patauá oil is trade wealth.

lookalikeNote: Bacaba's taller, greasier cousin — same genus. The oily feel of the fruit is the ID. Both safe.
name: Patauá
preparation: Eat the pulp fresh, or mash in warm water and skim the oil that rises — excellent cooking oil that keeps.

uses.note: pulp fresh or pressed for oil

codex: The palm that feeds the beetles that feed you. Inajá fruit falls, the weevils come, and the grubs are the real harvest.
description: a stout palm with a swollen trunk base and large bunches of yellow-orange plum-like fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Inajá. Yellow fruit bunches on a fat-based palm.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat). Fallen fruit draws palm weevils.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet oily pulp. The fallen fruit is bait — come back in a week for the grubs, which are pure fat.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the weevil grubs are the higher-value crop. Manage an inajá grove like a grub farm and you'll never lack fat.

lookalikeNote: The swollen trunk base is distinctive. The fruit resembles small plums; nothing toxic shares the shape and the palm.
name: Inajá
preparation: Eat the ripe yellow-orange pulp fresh. Leave fallen fruit as weevil bait — harvest the grubs days later.

uses.note: ripe pulp fresh
palm weevil grubs from fallen fruit

codex: Butter that grows on a spiny palm. The seed is half fat — the cosmetics industry pays fortunes for it; you'll eat it.
description: a short viciously spiny palm with bunches of yellow-brown fruit like small coconuts

knowledgeLevels.1: Murumuru. Spiny palm, coconut-like fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat), seed (crack for the fatty kernel).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the kernel is nearly half butter — dense calories. The pulp is sweet and filling.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the spines are the whole problem and the whole defense. Harvest with a pole; the seeds keep for months in the shell.

lookalikeNote: Tucumã's shorter, meaner cousin — both spiny, both safe. Murumuru fruit is bigger and the palm stays short.
name: Murumuru
preparation: Eat the pulp fresh; crack the hard seed for the fatty kernel — eat raw or render into butter.

uses.note: pulp and fatty seed kernel

codex: Delicious and armed. The pulp is superb — and the seed wears a coat of tiny wooden daggers that will ruin your mouth if you bite.
description: a tall tree with green-orange fruit the size of an orange, hiding a spiny pit inside

knowledgeLevels.1: Piquiarana. Tasty fruit, dangerous pit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pulp (eat). The pit is armored — never bite it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: rich oily pulp, excellent calories. The spines on the endocarp are the whole lesson.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: scrape the pulp off with your teeth like the locals — never close your jaw on the pit. The seed inside is edible too, once you get past the armor.

lookalikeNote: No poisonous lookalike — the danger is built in. The thin woody spines covering the pit stick into lips and gums of the careless.
name: Piquiarana
preparation: Eat the oily pulp by scraping it off the pit with your teeth — NEVER bite through. The pit's endocarp is covered in thin sharp spines.

uses.note: pulp scraped from the spiny pit

codex: Two foods, one tree, and a poison in between. The apple is juice; the nut is a chemistry lesson you do not skip.
description: a spreading tree with pear-shaped juicy fruit, each one carrying a kidney-shaped nut underneath

knowledgeLevels.1: Cashew. Juicy apple on top, weird nut hanging below.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the apple (eat fresh, juice it). The nut is POISON until roasted.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the apple is sweet, astringent, and ferments in a day — juice it fast. The nut's shell holds caustic cardol oil, kin to poison ivy.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: roast the nuts IN the shell first — the heat destroys the cardol — then crack. Never handle raw shell oil with bare hands; it blisters.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else grows its nut outside the fruit. The apple is unmistakable — but the nut it carries is the trap.
name: Cashew
preparation: Eat the apple fresh or juiced within a day (it ferments fast). The nut MUST be roasted in its shell before cracking — the shell oil (cardol/urushiol) burns skin and mouth raw.
sources: The Old Foodie: The Cashew Nut

uses.note: apple fresh or juiced
nut only after roasting in shell

codex: The giant's pantry. The lily's seeds feed you, its stalks feed you — the whole plant is a meal wearing a flower.
description: enormous round floating leaves with upturned rims, some wide enough to hold a child

knowledgeLevels.1: Giant water lily. Huge floating leaves, night-blooming flowers.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds (dry and roast), stalks and rhizomes (cooked like vegetables).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the seeds dry and roast into a starchy snack, or grind into flour. The stalks cook like greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: gather the seed pods as the flowers fade. Sun-dry thoroughly — damp seeds rot, dry seeds keep for months.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else on the water is this size. The leaf undersides carry sharp spines — handle pads by the rim, not from below.
name: Giant Water Lily
preparation: Collect the seeds, sun-dry, then roast — they pop and puff into a starchy snack, or grind to flour. Cook stalks and rhizomes as vegetables.

uses.note: seeds dried and roasted, or ground to flour
stalks and rhizomes cooked

codex: The Amazon's own yam — not the African import. White-fleshed, delicate, and it climbs the trees if you let it.
description: a climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and knobby white tubers underground

knowledgeLevels.1: Cush-cush yam. Climbing vine, white tubers.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: tubers (cook). The vine dies back in the dry — mark the spot.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: starchy staple, mild and filling. Digs easier in the wet season when the ground is soft.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: replant the tuber tips and vine cuttings — a yam patch is a savings account that compounds.

lookalikeNote: Taro grows nearby in the wet spots — taro has arrowhead leaves on stalks from the base; yam climbs. Cook both thoroughly.
name: Cush-cush Yam
preparation: Dig the tubers, peel, and cook thoroughly — boil or roast until soft all the way through. Never eat raw.

uses.note: tubers peeled and cooked through

codex: The floodplain's potato. Taro loves standing water — and it will punish you with a mouthful of needles if you get impatient.
description: big arrowhead leaves on long stalks rising from muddy water, with starchy corms below

knowledgeLevels.1: Taro. Big leaves in the mud, starchy corms underneath.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: corms and young leaves — BOTH must be cooked. Raw taro is full of calcium oxalate needles.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the corm is dense staple starch. The itch in your throat means you undercooked it — boil longer, change the water.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: taro is the flood-season crop — it thrives where manioc drowns. Plant the corm tops in the receding flood and eat while others go hungry.

lookalikeNote: Wild elephant-ear relatives share the leaf shape and are far more irritating — only eat taro you planted or that a local confirms. The rule is absolute: cook it like you mean it.
name: Taro
preparation: Peel and boil the corms thoroughly (change the water once) — raw taro's oxalate crystals burn the mouth and throat. Young leaves need long boiling too.

uses.note: corms peeled, boiled well; young leaves boiled long

codex: Born in the Americas, feeding the world. The roça's easy child — plant a vine cutting, come back to dinner.
description: a sprawling vine with heart-shaped leaves and sweet orange-fleshed tubers

knowledgeLevels.1: Sweet potato. Vine, orange tubers, sweet.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: tubers (raw is fine, cooked is better), young leaves (cooked greens).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fast energy, vitamin A in the orange flesh. The leaves are decent greens — boil them.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the easiest crop in the Amazon — vine cuttings root in days. A roça of sweet potato is a month from planting to eating.

lookalikeNote: Ornamental morning-glory vines share the flower shape but not the tuber. Dig first, admire flowers later.
name: Sweet Potato
preparation: Eat raw if you must; roast or boil for the real meal. Young leaves are cooked greens.

uses.note: tubers raw or cooked; leaves as cooked greens

codex: The fast one. Papaya goes from seed to fruit in a year — the pioneer's fruit, first to colonize every clearing.
description: a soft-trunked small tree with a crown of huge lobed leaves and melon-like fruit hanging below

knowledgeLevels.1: Papaya. Soft trunk, big lobed leaves, melon fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit (eat). Unripe fruit has latex — cooks use it to tenderize meat.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: gentle on the stomach, good when you're recovering. The seeds are peppery — a few are fine, a handful is a purge.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: papaya marks fresh disturbance — it fruits within a year of a clearing. Follow the papaya to find where people were, recently.

lookalikeNote: Ripe is the rule — green papaya's latex irritates. Wait for yellow-orange skin and a sweet smell.
name: Papaya
preparation: Eat fully ripe (yellow-orange, fragrant) — scoop the flesh, spit or swallow the peppery seeds sparingly.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw
unripe latex as meat tenderizer

codex: The tree that shoots back. Assacu doesn't want to be eaten, climbed, burned, or stood under — respect all four.
description: a huge tree with a trunk studded in conical thorns and pumpkin-shaped pods that explode

knowledgeLevels.1: Assacu. Thorny trunk, exploding pods. Stay back.
knowledgeLevels.2: The pods burst at 240 km/h, firing seeds like shrapnel. The white latex blisters skin and blinds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none for eating — ever. The latex was dart poison. The wood makes canoes, if you dare fell it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: learn this tree the way you learn a cliff edge — by location, not by touch. Never shelter under one in the dry season, never burn its wood (the smoke bites).

lookalikeNote: The conical thorns are unmistakable — 'monkey-no-climb'. Nothing edible in the Amazon wears armor like this. If the trunk has thorns and the pods are pumpkin-shaped, walk away.
name: Assacu (Sandbox Tree)
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Seeds and latex are violently toxic — purgative at best, poisoning at worst. Don't climb (thorns), don't stand under ripe pods (explosive seeds at 150+ mph), don't get the latex in your eyes.
sources: Google Arts & Culture: Curiously Dangerous — The Sandbox Tree

codex: The pretty weed that kills. Mottled seeds like engraved beans — beautiful, and a few will stop your heart. The oil is safe; the seed is not.
description: a tall weed with star-shaped leaves and spiny pods holding beautiful mottled beans

knowledgeLevels.1: Castor bean. Star leaves, spiny pods, pretty mottled seeds.
knowledgeLevels.2: The seeds hold ricin — one of the most potent plant poisons known. A handful can kill an adult.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none raw. The pressed oil (properly processed) is safe — the poison stays in the mash, not the oil.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it colonizes every disturbed patch in the tropics. Learn it young, because it WILL grow by your camp.

lookalikeNote: The star-shaped leaves and mottled seeds are distinctive. It grows exactly where you'd camp — clearings, riverbanks, ruins. Check the ground before you let anyone forage casually.
name: Castor Bean
preparation: DO NOT EAT the seeds — they contain ricin; even a few chewed seeds can be fatal. Only properly heat-processed castor oil is safe.

codex: The emergent giant's seeds are oil and protein — and chemistry that doesn't belong in a stomach. The fiber built life jackets; the seeds build nothing edible.
description: a towering emergent tree with a buttressed trunk, dropping pods full of silky fiber and dark seeds

knowledgeLevels.1: Kapok. Giant tree, silky pods, dark seeds.
knowledgeLevels.2: The seeds carry cyclopropenoid fatty acids (malvalic, sterculic) — the oil is classed non-edible, good for soap and biodiesel, not for you.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the fiber is the treasure — buoyant, water-resistant, warm. Stuff pillows, insulate, caulk canoes.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: kapok emergents are landmarks and spirit-houses across the Amazon. Harvest the fallen fiber; leave the seeds.

lookalikeNote: The buttressed trunk and emergent crown are the ID. Don't confuse the seeds with any edible nut — the fiber gives them away.
name: Kapok Seeds
preparation: DO NOT EAT. The seeds contain cyclopropenoid fatty acids; the oil is treated as non-edible (used for biodiesel and soap). Harvest the silky fiber instead — superb insulation and stuffing.
sources: MDPI Plants: The Biology of the Genus Ceiba (2022 review)
ResearchGate: Chemical Composition of Kapok Seed

uses.note: silky fiber for insulation, stuffing, caulking

codex: Rubber built Manaus and Belém — and the seeds built nothing but trouble raw. Cyanide in a shell, dinner after a long boil.
description: a tall plantation tree with three-part leaves and three-lobed pods that explode, flinging large mottled seeds

knowledgeLevels.1: Rubber tree. Three-leaflet leaves, exploding pods.
knowledgeLevels.2: The seeds carry linamarin — cyanogenic, ~186 mg/kg. Raw, they're poison. Locals eat them only after thorough, long cooking.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: famine food at best. The latex is the real crop — tap it, don't eat it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the pods explode like the assacu's smaller cousins — gather seeds from the ground, and boil them like you mean it, twice.

lookalikeNote: The three-lobed exploding pods are shared with its cousins. Don't confuse the seeds with Brazil nuts — rubber seeds are mottled, flatter, and raw-poisonous.
name: Rubber Seeds
preparation: POISONOUS RAW (cyanogenic glycosides). Only edible after thorough prolonged cooking — the way riverside communities prepare them. When in doubt, leave them; this is famine food, not a snack.
sources: Universiti Sains Malaysia: rubber seed as food (IFRJ)

uses.note: only after thorough prolonged cooking — famine food

codex: The grain that feeds the Sahel. It grows on rain that other crops call a drought.
description: a tall grass with a dense bottle-brush grain head

knowledgeLevels.1: Pearl millet. Tall grass, dense grain head like a bottle brush. This is food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: grain heads (thresh, winnow, grind). Stalks are fodder and building material.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the Sahel's staple grain — porridge, couscous, flatbread. Drought-tough; it fruits where maize dies.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest when heads are hard and dry; thresh by beating, winnow in wind. Pound to flour; stores a year dry. 2x yield if you cut whole heads before birds do.

lookalikeNote: The grain head is a dense cylindrical spike, unmistakable once headed. Young shoots resemble any grass — wait for the head.
name: Pearl Millet
preparation: Thresh and winnow the grain; grind to flour. Cook as porridge or couscous — raw grain is indigestible.
sources: field notes: dominant Sahel staple grain

uses.note: thresh, grind, cook as porridge/couscous

codex: Sorghum waits out the dry season in a granary and outlasts every other plan.
description: a tall cane-like grass with a loose branching head of grain

knowledgeLevels.1: Sorghum. Tall as a person, grain in a branching head. Food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: grain (thresh and grind), sweet stalks (chew for juice), leaves (fodder).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: porridge, flatbread, brewing. The grain keeps for years dry — famine insurance.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: some varieties have bitter tannin coats — taste a grain first; the sweet-stalk types are the treat. Harvest whole panicles; thresh dry.

lookalikeNote: Tall cane-like stalks with a loose branching grain head — distinct from pearl millet's dense spike. Wild sorghums exist; the grain head shape is the tell.
name: Sorghum
preparation: Thresh, winnow, grind. Cook thoroughly as porridge or flatbread.

uses.note: grain for porridge/flatbread; sweet stalks chewed fresh

codex: The oldest cultivated grain in West Africa, and the fastest from seed to bowl.
description: a delicate low grass with tiny grains on finger-like heads

knowledgeLevels.1: Fonio. Small grass, tiny grains. The grains are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the tiny grains (pound to dehusk, winnow). Cooks in minutes.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: West Africa's ancient grain — porridge, couscous. Matures fast; the hungry-season bridge.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the grains are sand-sized — winnow carefully or you eat grit. Parboil then steam; 2x yield from a patient threshing.

lookalikeNote: Tiny grains on delicate finger-like seed heads. Resembles wild Digitaria grasses — the cultivated stands are planted in rows; wild ones scatter.
name: Fonio
preparation: Dehusk by pounding, winnow well, rinse. Cooks fast — porridge or steamed like couscous.
sources: field notes: West African Sahel grain

uses.note: dehusked grains cooked as porridge or couscous

codex: Beans for the grain, leaves for the pot — the vine that completes the millet.
description: a trailing vine with three-part leaves and long thin pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Cowpea. Vine, three-part leaves, long pods. The beans inside are food — cooked.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: dried beans (boil well), young leaves (greens), fresh pods (vegetable).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: protein to go with the grain — the Sahel's bean. Fixes nitrogen; planted with the millet.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: beans must be boiled until fully soft — undercooked beans punish you. Young leaves are the fastest green you'll get.

lookalikeNote: Climbing/trailing vine with trifoliate leaves and long thin pods. Pods resemble wild legumes — the plump cultivated pods are the tell.
name: Cowpea
preparation: Boil dried beans until completely soft. Never eat dried beans raw or undercooked.

uses.note: beans boiled soft; young leaves as greens

codex: Called groundnut here, peanut elsewhere. Fat you can carry in your pocket.
description: a low bushy plant with paired oval leaves; nuts underground

knowledgeLevels.1: Groundnut. Low bush, nuts buried under it. Dig them up.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the nuts (roast or boil). Oil-rich — serious calories.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: roast for eating, pound for sauce, press for oil. Protein and fat together.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: NEVER eat moldy, shriveled, or bitter nuts — aflatoxin from bad storage is a slow poison. Roast fresh nuts; discard anything off-smelling.

lookalikeNote: Low bushy plant with paired oval leaflets; the nuts grow underground. Dig carefully — the shells are unmistakable, but moldy nuts are the real danger.
name: Peanut
preparation: Roast or boil fresh nuts. Discard any moldy, discolored, or bitter nuts — aflatoxin.
sources: field notes: aflatoxin risk in Sahel storage

uses.note: nuts roasted or boiled; pounded into sauce

codex: The tree of life, and it earns the name. Fruit in the hungry season, leaves for the pot, shade for the village.
description: a massive bottle-trunked tree, branches like roots against the sky

knowledgeLevels.1: Baobab. The upside-down tree. Everything it offers is food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: dry fruit pulp (tangy, vitamin C — eat dry or stir into water), young leaves (greens, cooked), seeds (roast).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the fruit is called monkey bread — powdery pulp eaten as-is or as a drink. Leaves make a mucilaginous sauce leaf. Vitamin C when nothing else has any.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruit ripens in the dry season — the hungry months. Crack the hard pod, shake out the dry pulp; no cooking needed. Leaves dried and pounded keep for the dry season.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable: a trunk like a water tower, branches like roots in the air. Nothing else looks like it.
name: Baobab
preparation: Eat the dry fruit pulp as-is or stirred into water. Cook young leaves as greens.

uses.note: dry fruit pulp eaten raw or as drink; leaves cooked as greens
vitamin C — scurvy prevention in the dry season

codex: Sour enough to wake the dead, sweet enough to keep you walking. The traveler's tree.
description: a broad shady tree with feathery leaves and hanging brown pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Tamarind. Big shady tree, brown pods. The sour pulp inside is food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe pod pulp (sour-sweet, eat fresh or soak into a drink), seeds (roast in famine).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: souring for sauces, a tart drink, travel food — the pulp keeps for months. Vitamin C and appetite when food is dull.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick pods that are brown and brittle; the pulp should pull away clean. Soak pulp, strain seeds — the drink keeps days.

lookalikeNote: Feathery compound leaves, brown curved pods hanging in clusters. The sour pulp inside is the tell — nothing poisonous mimics it.
name: Tamarind
preparation: Eat ripe pulp fresh or soak in water for a tart drink. Strain out seeds and fibers.

uses.note: ripe pulp eaten fresh or as a drink

codex: Sweet underground nuts that survive the dry season in the ground, waiting.
description: a grass-like sedge; striped nutty tubers underground

knowledgeLevels.1: Tiger nut. Sedge, tubers underground. Dig — the striped tubers are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the tubers (eat fresh, dried, or ground into a sweet milky drink).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet, chewy, filling — the original energy bar. The drink (kunun aya) is a meal in a cup.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: wash tubers well — grit is the enemy. Dry them for storage; soak dried ones overnight before eating.

lookalikeNote: Grass-like sedge with triangular stems; the tubers are small striped nuts underground. Other sedges look identical above ground — dig to confirm.
name: Tiger Nut
preparation: Wash well. Eat fresh, dried, or ground and soaked into a sweet drink.

uses.note: tubers fresh, dried, or as a ground drink

codex: The pod that holds a sauce together. Slimy is the point.
description: a hibiscus-like plant with ridged green pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Okra. Ridged green pods. Pick young pods — food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young pods (cook), leaves (greens), seeds (roast as coffee substitute in famine).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the pod's mucilage thickens sauces — the base of a thousand Sahel stews. Leaves are good greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick pods young and tender; old pods are woody string. Slice and sun-dry for the dry season.

lookalikeNote: Ridged green pods on a hibiscus-like plant. WARNING: thorn-apple (Datura) grows nearby with spiky round pods — compare carefully; okra pods are ridged and elongated, never round and spiny.
name: Okra
preparation: Cook young pods — stews, sauces. Sun-dry sliced pods for storage.

uses.note: young pods cooked; leaves as greens

codex: Red as sunset, sour as gossip. The drink of every market in the Sahel.
description: a tall plant with deep red fleshy calyces

knowledgeLevels.1: Bissap. Red fleshy cups around the seed pods. Those red calyces are food and drink.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: calyces (steep into tart red tea, hot or cold), leaves (sour greens).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: bissap — the Sahel's drink. Vitamin C, cooling, keeps in the heat. Leaves sour a sauce like tamarind.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest calyces when plump and deep red; dry them — dried bissap keeps a year and is trade goods.

lookalikeNote: Deep red fleshy calyces around a seed pod — unmistakable when fruiting. Leaves resemble okra's; the red calyx is the confirmation.
name: Bissap Hibiscus
preparation: Steep fresh or dried calyces in water for bissap tea. Cook leaves as sour greens.
sources: field notes: bissap is the Sahel's drink

uses.note: calyces as tea; leaves as sour greens
vitamin C; cooling drink in heat

codex: The tree that feeds you twice — leaves in the rains, pods in the dry.
description: a slender fast-growing tree with feathery leaves and long hanging pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Moringa. Feathery leaves, long pods. The leaves are food — fresh or dried.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (eat fresh, cooked, or dried and pounded to powder), pods (cook young), flowers (tea).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the most nutritious leaf in the Sahel — protein, iron, vitamins. Dried leaf powder keeps months and fortifies porridge.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: strip leaves, dry in shade (sun kills the vitamins), pound to powder. A spoonful a day in the hungry season.

lookalikeNote: Feathery twice-divided leaves, slender trunk, long ribbed pods. The drumstick pods are the tell.
name: Moringa
