preparation: Eat leaves fresh or cooked; dry and pound to powder for storage. Cook young pods.

uses.note: leaves fresh/cooked/dried; young pods cooked
iron, vitamin A — deficiency greens

codex: Gold you have to work for. The nuts are useless raw; the butter feeds a continent.
description: a broad gnarled tree with round green fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Shea. Gnarled tree, round fruits. The nuts inside need work before they're food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: nuts (process to butter — never eat raw), fruit pulp (eat fresh when ripe, sweet).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: shea butter — cooking fat, the Sahel's oil. The ripe fruit pulp is a sweet snack in season.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: boil nuts, sun-dry, crack, roast kernels, grind, knead with water — the butter rises. Days of work; months of fat.

lookalikeNote: Broad gnarled canopy, round green fruits ripening in the rains. The fruit pulp is sweet and safe fresh — the NUT is the part that needs processing.
name: Shea
preparation: NEVER eat raw nuts. Boil, dry, crack, roast, grind, knead — extract the butter. Eat ripe fruit pulp fresh.
sources: field notes: shea parklands, women's harvest

uses.note: nuts processed to butter; ripe fruit pulp eaten fresh

codex: Sweet, bitter, and stubborn — the tree that fruits when nothing else dares.
description: a spiny evergreen tree with plum-sized yellow-brown fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Desert date. Spiny tree, plum-sized fruits. The ripe pulp is food — bittersweet.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit pulp (eat fresh or dried), young leaves (boil as vegetable), kernel (crack the stone, roast — oily).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: pulp is candy in the dry season; kernel oil cooks and the kernel meal feeds stock. Leaves are famine greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: ripe = yellow-brown and fragrant; green fruit is harsh. Soak fruit, wash off pulp, sun-dry the stones, crack for kernels — stone-on-stone work.

lookalikeNote: Spiny branches, plum-sized faintly five-grooved fruits ripening yellow-brown. Green fruit is harsh — wait for the color change.
name: Desert Date
preparation: Eat ripe pulp fresh or dried. Boil young leaves. Crack stones for kernels; roast them.
sources: MDPI Foods 2023 — Balanites aegyptiaca kernel oil (Sahel/Sahara uses)

uses.note: ripe pulp fresh/dried; leaves boiled; kernels roasted
pulp used traditionally for cough, constipation

codex: The bush by every path, fruiting in the worst months. The Sahel's candy store.
description: a thorny bush with small round yellow-red fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Jujube. Thorny bush, small round fruits. Ripe ones are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruits (eat fresh, dry for later), leaves (fodder, tea).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet-tart snack, dried into a travel food. Fruits in the dry season when little else does.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick when deep yellow to red and slightly wrinkled — fully ripe. Dry in the sun; dried jujubes keep months.

lookalikeNote: Thorny zigzag branches, small round fruits ripening yellow to red. Ripe fruit is safe; unripe green ones are just sour, not dangerous.
name: Jujube
preparation: Eat ripe fruit fresh or sun-dried.

uses.note: ripe fruits fresh or dried

codex: Small white berries on a dusty bush — the children's harvest.
description: a dusty grey-green bush with small white-pink berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Grewia. Grey-green bush, small pale berries. The ripe berries are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe berries (eat fresh; pound with water into a drink), leaves (famine greens).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: called godeim — the berries make a sweet drink; children live on them in season. Iron-rich.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: berries ripen white to pinkish — taste for sweetness. Pound, soak, strain; the juice is the prize.

lookalikeNote: Small shrub with rough grey-green leaves and pea-sized pale berries. Ripe berries are sweet — sour or bitter ones aren't ready.
name: White Crossberry
preparation: Eat ripe berries fresh or pounded into a drink.
sources: Sudan National Food Research Centre — indigenous fruits (godeim)

uses.note: ripe berries fresh or as a drink

codex: The weed that feeds. It volunteers in every disturbed patch of ground.
description: a fast leafy green, sometimes reddish stems

knowledgeLevels.1: Amaranth. Leafy green, fast-growing. The young leaves are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves and shoots (cook as greens), seeds (grain — thresh like millet, smaller).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: alefu — the everyday green. Iron and protein when the grain runs thin. Seeds are a bonus grain.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick young tops before flowering; older leaves get tough. The seeds ripen after the leaves are done — two harvests, one plant.

lookalikeNote: Fast-growing leafy green with a dense flower spike. Young plants resemble other weeds — the grain-like seed head at maturity confirms it.
name: African Amaranth
preparation: Cook young leaves as greens. Thresh seeds as a grain.

uses.note: young leaves cooked; seeds as grain

codex: Tree tears you can eat. The Sahel's oldest export is food if you know which wound to tap.
description: a thorny acacia; amber gum oozing from bark wounds

knowledgeLevels.1: Gum acacia. Thorny tree, amber tears on the bark. The gum is food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: gum tears (dissolve in water — a sustaining drink), seeds (famine food, cooked), pods (fodder).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: gum arabic — dissolved, it's calories and calm for an empty stomach. A handful of gum and water is a meal's ghost.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: collect tears that are hard and clear; tap by wounding bark in the dry season and return in days. The pale tears are the cleanest.

lookalikeNote: Thorny acacia with paired white thorns; amber gum tears on wounded bark. Other acacias gum too — the pale hard tears of this one are the food grade.
name: Gum Acacia
preparation: Dissolve clean gum tears in water as a drink. Cook seeds in famine.

uses.note: gum dissolved in water; seeds cooked in famine

codex: Medicine with teeth. It cures at a spoonful and punishes at a bowlful.
description: a fast tree with feathery leaves and bitter smell

knowledgeLevels.1: Neem. Feathery leaves, bitter smell. Medicine, not food — small amounts only.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves and bark (bitter tea — fever, malaria tradition), twigs (chewing sticks), seeds (oil — NOT food).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the Sahel's pharmacy tree — fever tea, wound wash, tooth sticks. The bitterness is the dose talking.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: a small handful of leaves steeped, not boiled to death. Large doses of leaves or any seed oil are toxic — this is a medicine with a ceiling.

lookalikeNote: Feathery compound leaves with a bitter garlic-onion smell when crushed, small white flowers, olive-like fruits. The bitter smell is the tell — moringa, which looks similar, smells like nothing.
name: Neem
preparation: Steep a small handful of leaves as a bitter tea. Never ingest seed oil. Chew twigs as tooth sticks.

uses.note: bitter leaf tea for fever; twigs as tooth sticks

codex: A palm that fruits where the groundwater runs, and feeds the villages along the river.
description: a clustering palm with orange date-like fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Senegal date palm. Clustering palm, orange fruits. The ripe fruits are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruits (eat fresh — sweet pulp around a hard seed), palm heart (famine food, kills the stem), young shoots (vegetable).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the wild date of the riverbanks — sweet, filling, reliable. The heart is a last-resort meal; taking it kills that stem.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: fruits ripen orange and soft; green ones are astringent. Clusters keep on the tree for weeks — harvest as needed.

lookalikeNote: Clustering palm (many stems) with feathery fronds and orange date clusters. Green unripe fruits are astringent but not dangerous — wait for orange.
name: Senegal Date Palm
preparation: Eat ripe orange fruits fresh. Cook young shoots as vegetable.

uses.note: ripe fruits fresh; young shoots as vegetable

codex: Gingerbread you have to gnaw. The doum fruits when the river remembers it.
description: a forked palm with fan leaves and large brown gingerbread-smelling fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Doum palm. Forked trunk, fan leaves. The brown fruits are food — gnaw the rind.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit rind (gnaw the sweet fibrous flesh; soak pounded rind for a sweet drink), unripe kernel (crack green fruit for the white nut), germinated shoots (vegetable).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the gingerbread tree — the rind tastes of spice and honey. Pounded rind soaked in water makes a brown sweet juice for millet cakes.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: green fruit hides a white edible kernel — crack it young. Ripe fruit: chew the rind, spit the fiber, or pound and soak for juice. The hard seed is vegetable ivory, not food.

lookalikeNote: The only palm that forks — Y-shaped trunk, fan leaves. Large brown woody fruits. Unmistakable.
name: Doum Palm
preparation: Gnaw ripe rind; pound rind and soak for sweet juice. Crack green fruit for the white kernel.

uses.note: rind gnawed or soaked for juice; green kernels

codex: The melon is a lie; the seeds are the truth. Bitter enough to kill, rich enough to live on.
description: a trailing vine with yellow-green melon-sized fruits

knowledgeLevels.1: Egusi melon. Vine, melon-sized fruits. The FRUIT is poison-bitter — the SEEDS are food, cooked.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds (separate from the pulp, wash, roast or boil well — the famous egusi). The flesh is violently bitter and purgative.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: egusi soup — the seeds ground into a rich thick soup, protein and oil. Famine food of the Sahara for millennia.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest ripe, crack, scoop seeds, wash them free of pulp, sun-dry, then roast. The bitter flesh never goes in the pot — not a scrap.

lookalikeNote: Looks EXACTLY like a small watermelon — yellow-green rind, melon size. Taste a crumb of flesh: watermelon is sweet, egusi is unspeakably bitter. The bitterness is the warning. Never confuse the two.
name: Egusi Melon
preparation: Separate seeds from bitter pulp; wash, dry, roast or boil thoroughly. Never eat the flesh.
sources: Wikipedia — Citrullus colocynthis (culinary: seeds separated and thoroughly cooked)
phys.org 2022 — ancient egusi seed use, Libya/Sudan

uses.note: seeds washed and cooked — egusi soup base

codex: Bitter as regret, good as medicine. The washing is the cooking.
description: a shrub with dark green slightly bitter-smelling leaves

knowledgeLevels.1: Bitter leaf. Shrub, dark leaves. The leaves are food — but only after washing the bitter out.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (squeeze-wash repeatedly, then boil — the classic soup leaf).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the great West African soup leaf — nutrition under the bitterness. Also a fever tea in small amounts.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pound or squeeze the leaves in water, change the water, repeat until the bitterness is bearable. Boil after washing. Under-washed leaves are a stomach ache, not a meal.

lookalikeNote: Shrub with dark green elliptical leaves, intensely bitter when crushed. The bitterness itself is the ID — sweet lookalikes don't punish you for skipping the wash.
name: Bitter Leaf
preparation: Squeeze-wash leaves in several changes of water, then boil. Never eat unwashed.
sources: Frontiers in Natural Products 2024 — Vernonia amygdalina review
European J. Food Sci. Tech. — debittering methods

uses.note: leaves squeeze-washed and boiled
fever tea, small amounts

codex: The root that feeds half a billion people — and poisons anyone in a hurry.
description: a woody shrub with starchy tuberous roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Cassava. Shrub, thick roots. The roots are food ONLY after proper processing.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: roots (peel completely, soak/ferment, then cook thoroughly). Leaves (boil well — also cyanogenic raw).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the calorie backbone — garri, fufu, éba. But bitter varieties carry cyanide; the processing is not optional.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: peel all skin, soak peeled roots in water (change it), ferment sour, then roast or boil. Sweet varieties need peeling + thorough cooking; bitter ones need the full soak-ferment. Hungry shortcuts have killed people — WHO counts ~200 deaths a year from bad processing.

lookalikeNote: Woody shrub with palmate leaves and thick roots. Sweet vs bitter varieties look identical — treat every root as bitter until you know the planting. The rule is the processing, not the variety.
name: Cassava
preparation: Peel completely, soak/ferment in changed water, then cook thoroughly. Never eat raw or under-processed.

uses.note: roots peeled, soaked/fermented, cooked — garri/fufu

codex: Pound it and it becomes a meal you can hold. The yam barn is the bank.
description: a climbing vine with large starchy tubers underground

knowledgeLevels.1: Yam. Climbing vine, huge tubers. The tubers are food — cooked.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: tubers (boil, roast, or pound into fufu). Never raw — raw yam is harsh and some wild kinds are toxic.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: pounded yam — the feast food. Roasted yam is travel food. A barn of yams is wealth you can eat.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest by digging carefully — broken tubers rot. Cure in shade; store in an airy barn. Boil or roast fully; pounding is for the celebration.

lookalikeNote: Climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and massive tubers. Cultivated yams are the food — wild yams in the bush can be bitter and toxic; don't dig at random.
name: White Yam
preparation: Boil, roast, or pound fully cooked. Never eat raw.

uses.note: tubers boiled/roasted/pounded

codex: The lily that feeds the floodplain. Roots in the mud, dinner on the plate.
description: broad floating leaves and white-blue flowers on still water

knowledgeLevels.1: Water lily. Floating leaves, showy flowers. The tubers and seeds are food — cooked.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: rhizomes/tubers (dig from mud, boil), seeds (dry, grind or pop like grain).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: floodplain food — tubers when the water drops, seeds when it flowers. Filling starch.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: feel for tubers in the mud with your feet; boil well. Dry seeds fully before grinding.

lookalikeNote: Floating round leaves with a notch, white to blue flowers. The edible tubers are underwater — confirm by digging, not by the flower.
name: Water Lily
preparation: Boil tubers from the mud. Dry and grind seeds.

uses.note: tubers boiled; seeds dried and ground

codex: Rice's wild ancestor, still feeding the floodplains it came from.
description: a tall wild grass with rice-like grains, standing in shallow water

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild rice. Tall grass in shallow water, rice-like grains. The grains are food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: grains (knock into a canoe or basket, winnow, parch, cook).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the Niger floodplain's grain — harvested from boats by knocking ripe heads. Nutty, filling, free.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest by bending heads over a basket and beating — the ripe grains fall. Parch to loosen husks, winnow, then cook like rice. Shallow water only; deep water is for fish.

lookalikeNote: Tall grass in standing water with rice-like panicles. Resembles cultivated rice — the wild stands are in natural floodplain, unplanted rows.
name: African Wild Rice
preparation: Knock ripe grains into a basket, winnow, parch, cook.
sources: field notes: Niger inner delta grain

uses.note: grains knocked, winnowed, parched, cooked

codex: The famine berry. Bitter, small, and there when nothing else is.
description: a tough evergreen shrub with small round berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Hanza. Tough shrub, small round berries. The ripe berries are famine food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (soak to remove bitterness, then eat or dry), leaves (famine greens, cooked).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: called hanza — the berries carry villages through the hungry season. Bitter raw; soaking tames them.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: soak berries in several changes of water to debitter, then dry. The bitterness is the price of a free harvest.

lookalikeNote: Evergreen shrub with small round green-to-yellow berries. Bitter when raw — the soaking is the preparation, not a warning sign of poison.
name: Hanza
preparation: Soak berries in changed water to debitter, then eat or dry.

uses.note: berries soaked to debitter, eaten or dried

codex: Pretty as an apple, honest as a lie. Everything about it is poison.
description: a grey-green shrub with apple-sized green fruits and milky sap

knowledgeLevels.1: Sodom apple. Grey-green shrub, apple-sized green fruits. DO NOT EAT. The sap burns.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: none are food. The milky latex blisters skin and blinds eyes; the fruit's cardiac poisons stop hearts.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none for the pot. Traditional medicine uses it in expert hands only — the margin between dose and death is a whisper.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: recognize it at a glance — thick grey-green leaves, inflated apple-like green fruits, white latex from any cut. Teach everyone. This is the plant that kills the curious.

lookalikeNote: THIS IS THE LOOKALIKE WARNING: the green apple-sized fruits look like food from a distance. They are not. Milky latex from any cut = walk away. Nothing edible in the Sahel bleeds white like this.
name: Sodom Apple
preparation: No preparation makes it food. Avoid entirely.
sources: PMC — ocular toxicity of Calotropis latex

codex: The living fence with murder in its seeds. One to three seeds hospitalize; children die.
description: a small tree with lobed leaves and black seeds in three-part pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Physic nut. Small tree, often planted as a living fence. The seeds are POISON.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: none are food. Seeds carry curcin and phorbol esters — 1–3 seeds poison an adult, fewer kill a child.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none for the pot. The oil burns in lamps and runs engines; the seed cake kills rats. That is its job.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the living fences around fields are physic nut — teach children by name. The black seeds look like small chestnuts; the resemblance is the trap.

lookalikeNote: Planted in rows as living fences — lobed leaves, yellow-green three-part fruits, black seeds. The seeds look like small edible chestnuts. They are not. Fence rows = warning rows.
name: Physic Nut
preparation: No preparation makes it food. Avoid entirely.
sources: FAO — Jatropha curcas toxicity (1-3 seeds toxic)

codex: The trumpet flower that unmakes minds. Beautiful, common, and utterly not food.
description: a weed with trumpet flowers and spiny round pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Thorn apple. Trumpet flowers, spiny round pods. POISON — every part.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: none are food. Tropane alkaloids — delirium, racing heart, death. The seeds are the worst.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none for the pot. This is the plant that steals minds; there is no safe dose for the hungry.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the spiny round pods grow near okra fields and look vaguely like okra's cousins. They are not cousins. Okra pods are ridged and elongated; thorn-apple pods are round and spiny. When in doubt, the trumpet flower decides — walk away.

lookalikeNote: CRITICAL LOOKALIKE: spiny round pods vs okra's ridged elongated pods. Same fields, same season. Check the pod shape, check for the trumpet flower. A mistake here is a funeral.
name: Thorn Apple
preparation: No preparation makes it food. Avoid entirely.

codex: The king of fruit in this land. Ripe is perfume and honey; unripe is sour enough for pickles. The sap in the skin can rash sensitive skin — peel it.
description: a tree heavy with smooth-skinned fruit blushing red and gold

knowledgeLevels.1: Mango. Sweet, fragrant, stains everything yellow. The king of fruit here.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe flesh (eat), unripe (sour — chutneys, pickles), the big flat stone (plant it). Peel the skin — the sap rashes some people.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~120 kcal a fruit, rich in vitamin A and C. Unripe mango with salt and water steadies you in the hot-season heat.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick at the blush stage and ripen in straw or rice husk. A grafted tree keeps its variety; a seedling is a lottery. The stone planted at the rains becomes a tree in ten years.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable when ripe. At a distance the round orange fruit can suggest nux-vomica (nux_vomica) — check the leaves: mango has long lance-shaped alternate leaves and oblong fruit, never a perfect ball; nux-vomica has opposite oval leaves and flat coin seeds inside.
name: Mango
preparation: Eat ripe raw. Unripe: slice for chutney or pickle. Peel the skin — the sap irritates some people.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw; unripe for chutney/pickle
vitamin A and C; unripe + salt for heat

codex: The biggest tree-fruit on earth. Sweet bulbs inside when ripe; the seeds boil like chestnuts; unripe flesh cooks like meat. Oil your knife — the latex glues everything.
description: a tree carrying huge knobbly green pods, some bigger than your head

knowledgeLevels.1: Jackfruit. Enormous, knobbly, sweet inside. One fruit feeds a family.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe bulbs (eat), seeds (boil/roast — chestnut-like), unripe flesh (cooks like meat). Oil your knife and hands — the latex glues everything shut.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~150 kcal a chunk; the boiled seeds are a starchy staple. A single tree fruits for months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: tap for a hollow thump and sniff the stem — ripe smells sweet. Dry the seeds; they store for months. Roast before grinding into flour.

lookalikeNote: Nothing else grows fruit this size on a trunk. Breadfruit is the smaller, rounder cousin — same rules apply.
name: Jackfruit
preparation: Ripe: pull the bulbs, eat. Seeds: boil or roast 30 min. Unripe: cook as a vegetable. Oil hands and blade against the latex.

uses.note: ripe bulbs raw; seeds boiled/roasted; unripe cooked

codex: The traveler's canteen: sterile-ish water when young, rich meat when mature. Husk for fiber, shell for bowls and charcoal, oil that never spoils.
description: a tall leaning palm, green nuts clustered under the crown

knowledgeLevels.1: Coconut. Water inside, meat inside that. Never go thirsty near a palm.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: water (drink young), meat (eat; grate and press for milk), husk (fiber), shell (bowls, charcoal). Young = water; mature = meat.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~350 kcal of meat per nut; the water hydrates safely. Pressed oil keeps without spoiling and burns in lamps.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shake for slosh (young) or heft for weight (mature). A bearing palm drops year-round — mark the good ones and climb with a rope loop, never bare.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable. Fallen old nuts may be sprouted — the spongy 'apple' inside is edible too.
name: Coconut
preparation: Young (sloshes): drink the water, scoop the jelly. Mature (heavy, no slosh): crack for meat; grate and press for milk.

uses.note: water and meat; milk pressed from grated meat
young coconut water is safe to drink

codex: Rice gone feral in the drowned paddies. The staple of half the world, waiting in the mud — but the husk is silica glass. Husk it or it husks you.
description: a flooded flat of grass-like stalks hung with grain heads

knowledgeLevels.1: Rice, gone feral in the old paddies. The staple of half the world.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: grain only — pound and winnow off the husk first. The husk is inedible silica; eating unhusked paddy injures the gut.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~200 kcal a scoop cooked; the calorie backbone of every meal. Stores dry for a year.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest when heads droop and grains harden; sun-dry on mats before storing or it molds. One guarded paddy feeds many through the cool season.

lookalikeNote: Young rice looks like a dozen wild grasses — wait for the grain heads. No other grass here makes a fat white grain.
name: Feral Paddy Rice
preparation: Husk: pound and winnow until no husk remains. Boil. NEVER eat unhusked paddy — the husk tears the gut.

uses.note: husked and boiled; the staple grain

codex: Chana. Protein in a pod, from the cool-season fields. Soak overnight and boil soft — raw dried chickpeas are gravel and will not hurry.
description: a low bushy plant with small round pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Chickpea (chana). Protein in a pod.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds — soak overnight, boil till soft. Raw dried chickpeas are hard as gravel and will not cook fast.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~180 kcal a handful cooked; protein and fiber that keeps you full. Roasted, they keep for weeks in a dry bag.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the leaves sweat a sour acid (malic) — the old hands collected it for thirst on hot marches. Harvest fully dry or the pods mold in the bag.

lookalikeNote: The pods are distinctive — small, inflated, one or two round seeds. Rosary pea (rosary_pea) is a VINE with scarlet-black beads, never a pod like this.
name: Chickpea
preparation: Soak overnight, boil until soft (an hour or more). Roast for a keeping snack.

uses.note: soaked and boiled; roasted for storage

codex: Masoor dal. The fastest-cooking protein in the land — twenty minutes, no soaking. The broth alone has fed the sick for centuries.
description: a low feathery plant with tiny flat pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Masoor dal — the red lentil. Cooks faster than anything else in the field.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds — boil 20 minutes, no soaking. The skins slip when done; winnow out stones and chaff.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~170 kcal a handful; the fastest protein here. The broth feeds the sick when nothing else stays down.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: dry thoroughly before bagging — weevils are the enemy. A cool-season field of masoor is worth guarding like rice.

lookalikeNote: Do NOT confuse the pods with rosary pea (rosary_pea) — the pretty scarlet-black 'beans' are abrin poison, not lentils. No food bean is scarlet with a black eye.
name: Masoor Lentil
preparation: Boil 20 minutes until soft; no soaking needed. Skim and winnow out stones and chaff.

uses.note: boiled 20 min; the quick staple legume

codex: Haldi. The orange root that stains everything it touches — food, fingers, wounds. The old field dressing for cuts, and a pinch goes in every pot.
description: a clump of broad leaves; under it, orange fingers of root

knowledgeLevels.1: Turmeric (haldi). The orange root that stains everything it touches.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: rhizome — boil, dry, grind; or grate fresh into food. Fresh stains; dried keeps for months.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: antiseptic on wounds (the old field dressing), anti-inflammatory in food. A pinch in every pot.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cure the rhizomes — boil 45 minutes, sun-dry a full week — or they rot in the bag. Powder with a little oil and black pepper; the body takes it up far better.

lookalikeNote: Ginger (ginger) grows beside it and looks similar — ginger is pale and hot-tasting; turmeric is orange and earthy-bitter. Both are safe; confusing them only ruins the recipe.
name: Turmeric
preparation: Boil the rhizome, sun-dry, grind — or grate fresh into food. Fresh stains skin and cloth.

uses.note: spice; fresh grated or dried powder
antiseptic wound dusting; anti-inflammatory

codex: The monsoon berry. Sweet-tart, purple to the elbow. Ripe is deep purple and soft; red is a day early. Ferments by noon — eat or dry fast.
description: a big tree dropping purple-black berries that stain your tongue

knowledgeLevels.1: Jamun. The monsoon berry — sweet-tart, purple to the elbow.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat ripe — deep purple, not red), seed (dry and powder — the old blood-sugar remedy). Eat the fruit, spit the seed.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~60 kcal a handful; iron and vitamin C. The seed powder is medicine, not food.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shake the branches onto a cloth at dawn — the ripe ones fall on their own. They ferment by noon; eat fresh or sun-dry.

lookalikeNote: Ripe jamun is deep purple-black and soft, on a TREE. Lantana (lantana) berries cluster at the same season in mixed red-orange-purple — smaller, harder, on a rough-leafed SHRUB with square stems. Tree vs shrub is the test.
name: Jamun
preparation: Eat ripe and soft; spit the seed. Dry surplus in the sun — they keep weeks.

uses.note: ripe fruit raw; dried for storage
iron, vitamin C; seed powder is the folk blood-sugar remedy

codex: Bel. The hard-shelled fruit you crack like a coconut. Ripe pulp eats like custard; unripe dried and powdered is the classic dysentery cure of this land.
description: a thorny tree with hard round green-grey fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Bael (bel). The hard-shelled fruit — crack it like a coconut.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe pulp (eat; aromatic, yields to the thumb), unripe (sun-dry, powder — the dysentery cure), leaves (bitter tea). Strain out the gummy seeds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~90 kcal a half-fruit; the unripe powder stops dysentery — a life-saver where the water is dirty.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the shell keeps it fresh for weeks on the tree — a living pantry. Thorns mean harvest with a hooked stick, not bare hands.

lookalikeNote: Nux-vomica (nux_vomica) hangs round hard ORANGE fruit at the same season — its seeds are flat grey coins of strychnine. Bael is green-grey and larger; cracked open, bael seeds are small and woolly, never flat coins. When in doubt, don't.
name: Bael
preparation: Crack the shell, scoop the pulp, strain out gummy seeds. Unripe: slice, sun-dry, powder for dysentery.

uses.note: ripe pulp raw
unripe powder for dysentery

codex: Amla. Sour enough to make your eyes water — and one of the richest vitamin C sources on earth. It keeps its C even dried, which is why the old hands prize it.
description: a tree with feathery leaflets and pale green round fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Amla. Eye-wateringly sour — and one of the richest vitamin C sources on earth.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit (eat fresh if brave; better dried, pickled, or boiled with jaggery). The sour IS the medicine.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: preserves vitamin C even dried — the old scurvy cure of this land. A winter handful keeps gums and wounds sound.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest before the fruit drops; shade-dry to keep the C. One tree's harvest, dried, lasts the year.

lookalikeNote: No twin — the feathery leaflets plus pale ribbed fruit are distinctive. If it isn't mouth-puckering, it isn't ripe amla.
name: Amla
preparation: Eat fresh, dry, pickle, or boil with jaggery. Shade-dry surplus for the year.

uses.note: fresh, dried, or pickled — the sour staple
vitamin C that survives drying

codex: The flowers fall like rain at dawn and taste like brown sugar — then they ferment. Dry them fast and they're storable sugar; the seeds press into lamp oil.
description: a big shady tree; at dawn the ground beneath is strewn with fleshy cream flowers

knowledgeLevels.1: Mahua. The flowers fall like rain and taste like brown sugar — then they ferment.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: flowers (dry in sun, then cook — raw heaps ferment within a day), seeds (press for oil — cooking and lamp oil), ripe fruit pulp (eat sparingly).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: dried flowers are storable sugar (~120 kcal a handful); the seed oil burns clean in lamps.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: gather at dawn before the bees and the boars. Dry on clean mats — moldy mahua is a stomach bomb. A good tree is worth a dawn patrol.

lookalikeNote: No twin — the dawn carpet of cream flowers under a big tree is unmistakable. If the flowers smell of liquor already, they're fermenting: dry or abandon.
name: Mahua
preparation: Sun-dry the fallen flowers the same day, then cook. Seeds: press for oil. Never eat moldy dried flowers.

uses.note: dried flowers cooked; the storable sugar
seed oil burns clean in lamps

codex: Kamal. The pond is a pantry: crisp starchy roots below, seeds above. Feel for the root with your feet — don't dive blind into old tanks.
description: a still pond sheeted with round leaves and pink flowers; below, the roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Lotus (kamal). The pond is a pantry — roots below, seeds above.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: rhizome (peel, slice, boil or fry — crisp and starchy), seeds (crack, boil; pick out the bitter green sprout), young leaves (wrap food, not food).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~80 kcal a root; steady starch where rice fails. The seeds store dry for months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: feel for the root in the mud with your feet — never dive blind in old tanks. Always leave a growing node; the pond feeds you again.

lookalikeNote: Water-lily pads look similar but lotus leaves stand ABOVE the water on stalks and the flowers are big and pink. Only lotus makes the fat edible root.
name: Lotus
preparation: Peel, slice, boil or fry the rhizome. Seeds: crack, remove the bitter green heart, boil.

uses.note: rhizome cooked; seeds boiled

codex: Pond popcorn. The black seeds pop white in a hot pan — the Bihar staple. The pads are armor: harvest with a hooked pole, never bare hands.
description: a pond of huge spiny pads; under them, spiny pods of black seeds

knowledgeLevels.1: Makhana (fox nut). Pond popcorn — the black seeds pop white in a hot pan.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: seeds only (roast/pop; raw they're hard shot). The pads are armor — harvest with a hooked pole, never bare hands.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~100 kcal a handful popped; light, and it keeps for months dry.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: grade by size — the big ones pop, the small ones grind into flour. A harvested pond re-seeds itself if you leave the small pods.

lookalikeNote: Don't confuse the pods with lotus pods — makhana pads are viciously spiny, lotus pads are smooth. The seeds are black marbles; nothing else here makes those.
name: Makhana (Fox Nut)
preparation: Crack the spiny pods, pop the seeds in a hot dry pan like popcorn. Raw seeds are inedible shot.

uses.note: seeds popped/roasted; the keeping pond grain

codex: Singhara. The pond's horned nut — sweet and crisp. Boil it always: raw nuts from still water carry liver flukes.
description: floating rosettes of leaves; under them, black horned nuts

knowledgeLevels.1: Singhara (water chestnut). The pond's horned nut — sweet and crisp.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: kernel only (boil 20 minutes, crack the horned shell). NEVER eat raw from still water — liver flukes.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~90 kcal a handful; the fasting food of the cool season, gentle and filling.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: rake the rosettes with a pole — the ripe nuts drop. Dry in shell for months; the horns protect the kernel.

lookalikeNote: The horned black shell is unmistakable. Trapa's horns are the ID — nothing edible or poisonous here copies them.
name: Water Chestnut
preparation: Boil 20 minutes, crack the horned shell, eat the kernel. Always cooked — never raw from still water.

uses.note: kernel boiled and cracked

codex: Crisp and sweet — after you boil the poison out. Raw shoots carry cyanide; slice thin, boil TWICE, discard the water. No shortcuts.
description: a clump of giant grass; after rain, pale spears push up

knowledgeLevels.1: Bamboo shoots. Crisp and sweet — after you boil the poison out.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young shoots only (peel to the tender core, slice thin, boil TWICE and discard the water — cyanogenic glycosides). Old shoots are wood.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~40 kcal a shoot; bulk and crunch in the hungry wet season.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest at knee height — taller is bitter wood. Ferment the surplus in brine; it keeps a year and the sour is gold in the cool season.

lookalikeNote: No twin — but the rule is absolute: any shoot eaten raw or single-boiled can poison. If you can't boil twice with fresh water, don't pick.
name: Bamboo Shoot
preparation: Peel to the tender core, slice thin, boil, DISCARD the water, boil again. Then cook as food. Raw is poison.

uses.note: double-boiled, then cooked

codex: Arbi. The corm is potato-like once you cook the sting out — raw, the needle crystals set your mouth on fire. Cook with something sour; acid tames the itch.
description: big heart-shaped leaves on stalks, like elephant ears

knowledgeLevels.1: Arbi (colocasia/taro). The corm is potato-like — once you cook the sting out.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: corms (boil whole, peel AFTER cooking), leaves (boil with something sour — the sour tames the itch). Raw = mouth on fire (oxalate needles).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~110 kcal a handful; the wet-season starch that grows where rice drowns.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cook with tamarind — acid dissolves the oxalate itch. Replant the tops; each corm becomes a clump.

lookalikeNote: Elephant-ear leaves are the ID. Wild aroids with similar leaves are ALL irritant raw — the rule 'boil whole, peel after, eat with sour' covers the whole family safely.
name: Colocasia (Arbi)
preparation: Boil or roast WHOLE until soft, peel after cooking. Leaves: boil with tamarind or another sour. Never eat raw.

uses.note: corms boiled whole; leaves boiled with sour

codex: Chaulai. The weed that feeds — greens now, grain later. Strip the tops and it bushes out; let one plant seed and next rains you have a field.
description: a knee-high weed with soft green leaves and a seedy spike

knowledgeLevels.1: Chaulai (wild amaranth). The weed that feeds — greens now, grain later.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (cook 5 minutes), seeds (rub the dry spikes, winnow, pop or grind — a handful of seed is a meal's worth).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: iron and vitamin A in the greens; the seeds are ~15% protein — real grain from a weed.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cut-and-come-again — strip the tops and it bushes out thicker. Let one plant go to seed for next rains.

lookalikeNote: Young plants resemble lambs quarters (lambs_quarters) — both are safe, so the confusion costs nothing.
name: Wild Amaranth
preparation: Leaves: boil or sauté 5 minutes. Seeds: rub dry spikes, winnow, pop like tiny grain or grind.

uses.note: leaves cooked; seeds popped/ground

codex: Kadi patta. Not food by the handful — the flavor that makes food food. Tempered in hot oil, the crackle means it's working.
description: a shrub with glossy leaflets that smell of curry when crushed

knowledgeLevels.1: Curry leaf (kadi patta). The flavor that makes food food.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (temper in hot oil — the crackle means it's working; or boil in water). Strip the bitter stems.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: iron and the appetite back — a handful in the pot stretches thin rations. The old stomach tonic.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shade-dries well; the powder keeps a year. Plant the berries — the birds plant them everywhere anyway.

lookalikeNote: Crush a leaf: curry leaf smells of curry, unmistakable. Neem leaves are bitter and larger — don't confuse the trees, though both are useful.
name: Curry Leaf
preparation: Fry in hot oil or boil in water. Chew a few raw for the stomach. Strip bitter stems.

uses.note: tempered in oil; the flavor base
iron; stomach tonic

codex: Tea and mosquito armor in one clump. Bruise the stalks and boil; rub crushed leaves on skin and the mosquitoes genuinely hesitate — for an hour.
description: a fountain of sharp-edged grass smelling of lemon

knowledgeLevels.1: Lemongrass. Tea and mosquito armor in one clump.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: stalks (bruise and boil), leaves (steep). The edges cut — harvest with a twist, never a bare grab.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the tea settles stomachs; the citronella oil genuinely repels mosquitoes for about an hour.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: split the clump to propagate — it divides like grass because it is grass. A ring around camp is worth more than a wall of it in the pot.

lookalikeNote: Lemon smell is the ID — crush and sniff. Scentless sharp grasses are just grass.
name: Lemongrass
preparation: Bruise stalks, boil 10 minutes for tea. Crushed leaves rubbed on skin repel mosquitoes.

uses.note: bruised stalks boiled
mosquito repellent; stomach-settling tea

codex: The courtyard herb. Tea for coughs, courage for fevers — and sacred to many households. Take only what you need, and say thanks.
description: a small bushy herb with purple-tinged leaves, smelling of cloves

knowledgeLevels.1: Tulsi (holy basil). The courtyard herb — tea for coughs.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (steep or chew), seeds (soak — they swell like frogspawn; the old cooling drink).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the household remedy for cough, cold, and low spirits. The smoke dislikes mosquitoes as much as you do.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pinch the flower heads and it bushes forever. It is sacred to many — harvest gently, never strip a courtyard plant bare.

lookalikeNote: Clove scent is the ID. Other basils are safe too — the confusion costs nothing.
name: Tulsi (Holy Basil)
preparation: Steep fresh or dried leaves in hot water. Chew a few for coughs. Seeds soaked make the cooling drink.

uses.note: steeped for coughs and fevers
household remedy; mosquito-disliking smoke

codex: Adrak. Heat without fire — for food and for guts. A thumb in the pot, a slice in the tea: the traveler's stomach insurance.
description: reed-like leaves; underground, knobby pale rhizomes

knowledgeLevels.1: Ginger (adrak). Heat without fire — for food and for guts.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: rhizome (fresh or dried). A thumb in the pot, a slice in the tea.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: settles nausea, warms the cold-season body. The first thing to reach for when the stomach turns.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: store in dry sand — it keeps for months. Replant a knob with an eye and it multiplies.

lookalikeNote: Turmeric (turmeric) grows beside it — ginger is pale and hot, turmeric orange and earthy. Both safe; confusing them only ruins the recipe.
name: Ginger
preparation: Grate fresh into food or boil for tea. Slice, sun-dry, and powder for the year.

uses.note: spice; fresh or dried
nausea; warming

codex: Bargad. A single tree that's a forest — and it fruits. Eat only the soft red ripe figs, and check for wasps first: a fig without wasps didn't ripen right.
description: the giant tree with roots dropping from its branches like curtains

knowledgeLevels.1: Banyan (bargad). A single tree that's a forest — and it fruits.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe figs only (soft, red — check for wasps first), aerial roots (fiber), bark (the old dysentery tea). Unripe figs are astringent and full of wasps.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~40 kcal a handful in fruit season; the deep shade is the real gift in the hot months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: sacred to many — harvest gently, take fallen fruit first. A fruiting banyan feeds every bird for a mile; watch what they eat.

lookalikeNote: Peepal (peepal_fig) fruits similarly — both are Ficus, both follow the same rules: ripe and soft only. The trees differ (banyan's curtain roots), the caution is identical.
name: Banyan Fig
preparation: Eat only fully ripe (soft, red) figs. Check for wasps. Unripe figs are astringent — leave them.

uses.note: ripe figs only

codex: The tree the Buddha sat under. Its figs feed the birds, and you in a pinch — ripe and soft only, and take fallen fruit first out of respect.
description: a tall tree with heart-shaped leaves that shiver in any breeze

knowledgeLevels.1: Peepal. The tree the Buddha sat under — its figs feed birds, and you in a pinch.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe figs (soft, dark — fallen fruit first), leaves (the shivering hearts are the ID), bark (bitter tea, medicine not food).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~35 kcal a handful; a hunger-gap fruit more than a staple.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: sacred to many — never cut, never strip. The figs come in waves; the birds will show you when.

lookalikeNote: Banyan (banyan_fig) is the cousin — same Ficus rules: ripe and soft only. Peepal's heart-shaped shivering leaves are the ID.
name: Peepal Fig
preparation: Eat only fully ripe fallen figs. Unripe figs are astringent.

uses.note: ripe fallen figs

codex: Taad. The pillar palm: jelly fruit in summer, sweet sap at dawn with a two-hour fuse — drink fresh or let it become toddy.
description: a towering fan palm, black and straight as a pillar

knowledgeLevels.1: Palmyra (taad). The pillar palm — jelly fruit in summer, sweet sap at dawn.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: fruit pulp (eat fresh — the jelly spoils by evening), sap/neera (drink within hours; it ferments to toddy fast), sprout (the tuber-like shoot, roast).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: ~80 kcal a fruit; the sap is sugar water with a two-hour fuse. The jaggery made from it keeps a year.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: tap at dawn, drink by noon. Eat the jelly in the field — it doesn't travel. The sprouts are the hidden harvest.

lookalikeNote: No twin — the black pillar trunk with a fan crown is unmistakable. Fallen fruit ferments fast; if it smells of liquor, abandon it.
name: Palmyra Palm
preparation: Eat the jelly pulp fresh the same day. Sap: drink within hours. Sprouts: roast.

uses.note: jelly pulp fresh; sap drunk within hours

codex: Putush. Pretty flowers, pretty berries — and the green ones can wreck your liver. The invader: where lantana thickets stand, the forest lost.
description: a scrambling shrub with rough leaves and clusters of tiny flowers in mixed colors

knowledgeLevels.1: Lantana (putush/ghaneri). Pretty flowers, pretty berries — and the green ones can wreck your liver.
knowledgeLevels.2: ID: square stems, rough sandpapery leaves that stink when crushed, flower heads mixing yellow-orange-pink. Berries green, then purple-black.
knowledgeLevels.3: Danger: unripe berries and leaves carry lantadenes — liver failure in livestock, misery in people. The ripe purple ones are less bad but NEVER safe.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it's the invader — where lantana thickets stand, the forest lost. Clear it for firewood; never for food. Goats that learn it, learn the hard way.

lookalikeNote: The berry clusters mimic jamun (jamun) at a hungry glance — but jamun is a TREE with single round purple fruit; lantana is a SHRUB with clustered mixed-color berries and rough stinking leaves. Tree vs shrub is the test.
name: Lantana
preparation: DO NOT EAT any part. If eaten: it was probably the berries — expect vomiting; watch the liver.
sources: Native Plant Society of Texas invasive profile

codex: Kuchila. The fruit looks friendly; the seeds are strychnine. Monkeys eat the pulp and spit the seeds — you are not a monkey. Learn this tree like a loaded gun.
description: a medium tree with glossy oval leaves and round orange fruit like small apples

knowledgeLevels.1: Poison-nut tree (kuchila). The fruit looks friendly. The seeds are strychnine.
knowledgeLevels.2: ID: opposite glossy oval leaves, foul-smelling greenish flowers, round hard orange fruit with jelly pulp and flat grey coin-seeds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Danger: seeds are ~1.5% strychnine — convulsions, and no antidote. Even the bark is poison. The pulp is eaten by monkeys and hornbills; the seeds pass through them whole.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: learn this tree the way you learn a loaded gun — by sight, at distance. Mark every one near camp and teach it to every newcomer.

lookalikeNote: Bael (bael) hangs hard round fruit at the same season — but bael is GREEN-GREY and larger, with small woolly seeds; nux-vomica is ORANGE with flat grey coin-seeds of strychnine. When in doubt, don't touch.
name: Strychnine Tree
preparation: DO NOT EAT any part. No safe preparation exists. Mark the tree; teach it.

codex: The trumpet-flower bush. Every part is a delirium poison — blindness, madness, death. No safe dose, no home antidote. It loves disturbed ground near ruins: exactly where you forage.
description: a bushy plant with big trumpet flowers, white or purple, and spiny round pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Datura. The trumpet-flower bush — every part is a delirium poison.
knowledgeLevels.2: ID: big trumpet blooms, spiny apple-like pods full of flat brown seeds. Smells rank when crushed.
knowledgeLevels.3: Danger: tropane alkaloids — dilated pupils, delirium, death. No safe dose and no home antidote. A single pod's seeds can kill.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it loves disturbed ground near ruins — exactly where you forage. Learn the trumpet at fifty paces; never touch the pods.

lookalikeNote: No edible twin in this land — that's the lesson. The pods tempt seed-collectors; the seeds inside are flat and brown, nothing like any food seed here.
name: Datura
preparation: DO NOT EAT any part. No safe preparation exists.

codex: Ratti. The prettiest poison here — beads red as blood with a black eye, once used to weigh gold. One chewed seed can kill an adult. No food bean is scarlet with a black eye.
description: a twining vine with feathery leaves and pods that split to show scarlet-black beads

knowledgeLevels.1: Rosary pea (ratti/gunja). The prettiest poison here — beads red as blood with a black eye.
knowledgeLevels.2: ID: twining vine, feathery leaflets, pods curling back to show hard shiny scarlet seeds with a black spot. Once used as the ratti gold-weight.
knowledgeLevels.3: Danger: abrin — one chewed seed can kill an adult, and there is no antidote. Intact seeds may pass through, but never gamble it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: children string them into beads; don't. If you see the beads, you're looking at a legume — and legumes are food here, which is exactly why this one kills the careless.

lookalikeNote: The seeds mimic small beans and lentils (masoor_lentil, chickpea) to a hungry eye — but no food bean is scarlet with a black eye. Color is the warning.
name: Rosary Pea
preparation: DO NOT EAT any part. No safe preparation exists. Do not string the seeds.

codex: The paddies went wild years ago. The rice didn't get the memo — it still heads, still fills, still feeds whoever bothers to thresh it.
description: a grass with drooping seed heads standing in shallow water

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild rice. A grass standing in the shallows with heavy seed heads.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the grain (thresh and winnow the heads). Needs cooking — boil like any rice.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: real calories, stores for months dry. Harvest when the heads droop and grains fall at a touch.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: beat the heads into a basket at dawn (dew keeps them from shattering early). Parboil before hulling. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Feral rice shatters — the grains fall at a touch when ripe. If the heads hold their grain tight, it's a planted variety gone weedy, still edible.
name: Feral Rice
preparation: Strip the heads, thresh, winnow, boil. The hulls are silica-sharp — winnow well.

uses.note: boiled grain; the region's staple starch

codex: The terraces went to seed but the bushes never stopped flushing. Two leaves and a bud — the old picking rhyme still works.
description: a waist-high bush with glossy oval leaves on terraced ground

knowledgeLevels.1: Tea bush. Glossy oval leaves, terraces gone wild.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the young flush — two leaves and a bud. Steep, don't gorge: caffeine and tannins.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: brewed tea for alertness and morale; chewed leaves for the trail. Wilt then heat the leaves to keep it green.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick at dawn in spring for the sweetest flush. Dry for storage. A rested mind forages better.

lookalikeNote: True tea has glossy evergreen leaves with finely serrated edges and a pale underside. If the leaf crushes without that clean tea smell, it's an imposter.
name: Tea Bush
preparation: Steep the young leaves; chew sparingly. Caffeine and tannins — a handful brewed is medicine, a basket eaten is a mistake.

uses.note: brewed; chewed sparingly on the trail
stimulant — alertness, morale

codex: Fall's candy, and it hangs on the tree into winter — nature's own pantry. The astringent ones teach patience; the ripe ones teach gratitude.
description: a tree hung with orange globes among broad dark leaves

knowledgeLevels.1: Persimmon. Orange fruit, still hard on the tree.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the fruit — eat only when soft and wrinkled. Unripe = a mouthful of chalk (tannins).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: high sugar, vitamin A and C. Hangs on the tree into winter — harvest through the cold months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: frost sweetens them. Dry halved ripe fruit for winter stores. 2x yield from the old orchard trees.

lookalikeNote: Wait for the fruit to go soft and wrinkled — or for frost. An unripe persimmon's tannins will turn your mouth inside out. Ripe ones are honey.
name: Asian Persimmon
preparation: Eat fully ripe (soft, wrinkled). Dry the ripe fruit for winter stores.

uses.note: ripe fruit fresh or dried

codex: A living fossil, planted at temples for a thousand years. The nut is food and a small poison both — the old rule is ten a day, roasted, and never for children.
description: a fan-leafed tree dropping foul-smelling yellow fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Ginkgo. Fan-shaped leaves, foul yellow fruit on the ground.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the inner kernel only. The flesh stinks and burns skin; the kernel must be roasted. Contains ginkgotoxin — dose matters.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: roasted kernels, ~10 a day max for adults. A documented poisoning case came from 50 roasted nuts — seizures. Respect the limit.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: crack, roast 25 minutes until the shell splits. Store dry. The street and temple trees are the reliable producers.

lookalikeNote: The fleshy outer coat stinks of rancid butter and blisters skin — wash the nuts with gloves or sticks, then crack and roast the inner kernel. Never eat the flesh.
name: Ginkgo Nut
preparation: Remove the stinking flesh, wash, roast or boil the kernel ~25 minutes. Limit: about 10 nuts a day for adults; children far fewer. Raw or excess nuts cause vomiting and seizures (ginkgotoxin, 4'-O-methylpyridoxine).

uses.note: roasted kernels, strictly limited

codex: The burrs do the guarding; the fire does the cooking. A chestnut lane in fall is a pantry with thorns.
description: a spreading tree with spiny green burrs splitting open in fall

knowledgeLevels.1: Chestnut. Spiny burrs splitting to show brown nuts.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the nut (score and roast; raw is tannic). Not the glossy horse chestnut — different tree, poisonous.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: roasted or boiled — real starch calories, stores weeks cool and dry. Gather fast; everything else wants them too.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: float-test in water (sinkers keep). Roast cut-side up. 2x yield from the old lane trees.

lookalikeNote: Horse chestnut (Aesculus) is NOT food: its seed is glossy mahogany with a big pale scar and no pointed tip, and it's bitter with saponins. True chestnut has a pointed tip and a small scar — roast it.
name: Chinese Chestnut
preparation: Score the shell, roast or boil. Raw chestnuts are tannic and hard to digest.

uses.note: roasted or boiled nuts

codex: The ancestor of every soybean on earth, still twining along the field edges. Protein that asks only for a pot and patience.
description: a twining vine with small hairy pods along field edges

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild soybean. A twining vine with small hairy pods.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the beans (small, dark). Must be cooked — raw beans upset the stomach badly.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: boiled or fermented — dense protein. The ancestor of tofu, miso, and soy sauce.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest when pods rattle. Long-cook with a pinch of ash to soften. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Small black seeds in hairy pods on a twining vine. If the pods are smooth and the vine doesn't twine, it's something else — check before you pick.
name: Wild Soybean
preparation: Boil the beans well — raw soybeans carry trypsin inhibitors that punish the gut. Ferment or long-cook.

uses.note: boiled or fermented beans

codex: Flower above, dinner below. The root keeps its crunch for months in cold mud — the pond is a root cellar that waters itself.
description: broad leaves standing tall above still water on stiff stalks

knowledgeLevels.1: Lotus. Big round leaves standing up out of still water.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the root (white, jointed, crunchy). Dig it from the mud under the standing leaves.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: starch and crunch — slice for soup, fry for chips. The seeds in the pod are food too.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: feel for the joints in the mud before you dig. Harvest in fall when the starch peaks. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Lotus leaves stand ABOVE the water on stiff stalks; water-lily pads float flat. Only the standing-leaf plant hides the crisp white root.
name: Lotus Root
preparation: Dig from the mud, peel, slice. Good raw, better cooked; the segments keep crisp in stir-fry.

uses.note: root fresh, boiled, or fried; seeds too

codex: The silvery underside is the signature — flip the leaf and it flashes white. Moxa, dumplings, and the taste of spring rain.
description: a knee-high herb with silvery-white leaf undersides

knowledgeLevels.1: Mugwort. Knee-high, silvery-white under the leaves.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the young shoots and leaves (pound into dumplings, dry for tea). Medicinal too — the old moxa herb.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: spring greens, stomach-settling tea. Harvest before it flowers for the tenderest tips.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: take the top 10cm only; it re-sprouts. Dry bundles for winter tea. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Flip the leaf: mugwort flashes silvery-white underneath and smells sharp-herbal when crushed. Young chrysanthemum looks similar but lacks the silver back — smell and flip before you pick.
name: Mugwort
preparation: Eat the young shoots fresh or pounded into dumplings; dry for tea. The silver underside is the ID.

uses.note: young shoots; dumplings and tea
stomach-settling tea; moxa herb

codex: The vine is the enemy and the root is the prize — three feet of starch hiding under the tangle. Kuzu: the thickener emperors ate.
description: a vast tangle of vines with huge leaves, roots like buried logs

knowledgeLevels.1: Kudzu. A tangle of vines swallowing the treeline.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the root — enormous, starchy. Dig in winter when the sap is down. The starch must be washed out and settled.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: kuzu starch for thickening, dumplings, noodles. The flowers make jelly; the young shoots are greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: follow the oldest vine to the crown root. Pound, wash, settle, dry — the white cake keeps for years. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Kudzu's leaves are big three-lobed affairs on a hairy vine. The prize is the crown root — dig where the oldest stem meets the ground.
name: Kudzu Root
preparation: Dig the root (winter is best), pound and wash the starch out, settle and dry. Cook the starch — dumplings, thickener, noodles.

uses.note: washed starch; dumplings and thickener

codex: The old mountain vegetable. Boil it, change the water, and respect the dose — bracken asks for moderation, not abstinence.
description: tightly coiled green fiddleheads unfurling into triangle fronds

knowledgeLevels.1: Bracken. Coiled fiddleheads opening into triangle fronds.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the young fiddleheads only. Boil and discard the water — bracken carries ptaquiloside, a carcinogen. Small amounts, rarely.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: a traditional spring vegetable across East Asia. Boiled, shocked, dressed. Never eat mature fronds.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick under 15cm, tight coils only. Double-boil for safety. A seasonal treat, not a staple.

lookalikeNote: True fiddleheads of bracken unfurl from fuzzy coils into triangular fronds. If the coil has a deep U-shaped groove and brown papery scales, that's ostrich fern — a different, safer fiddlehead.
name: Bracken Fiddlehead
preparation: Boil the young fiddleheads and discard the water (ptaquiloside). Eat sparingly and seasonally — never a daily staple.

uses.note: boiled fiddleheads, sparingly

codex: The invader that eats hillsides — and the spring vegetable that eats back. Tart as rhubarb, free as weeds.
description: red-speckled hollow shoots with heart-shaped leaves by the water

knowledgeLevels.1: Knotweed. Hollow red-speckled shoots by the water.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young shoots under 30cm, tart like rhubarb. Oxalic acid — don't live on it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: spring vegetable, jam, pie filling. Peel the older shoots.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: snap-clean shoots only. The patch you harvest is the patch you control. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Young knotweed shoots look like red asparagus with heart-shaped leaves. Only the young shoots are food — once the stems toughen and the leaves broaden, it's fiber, not dinner.
name: Knotweed Shoot
preparation: Eat young shoots raw or cooked; tart like rhubarb. Oxalic acid — moderate amounts.

uses.note: young shoots; tart vegetable

codex: Flat leaves, garlic breath. The dumpling herb — cut it and it comes back, cut it and it comes back.
description: a clump of flat grass-like leaves smelling of garlic when bruised

knowledgeLevels.1: Garlic chives. Flat leaves, garlic smell when bruised.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves and unopened buds. The smell is the ID — no garlic smell, no chive.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: dumplings, pancakes, stir-fry. Cut-and-come-again all season.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cut 5cm above the crown and it regrows in weeks. Divide clumps in fall. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: The garlic smell is the whole test: crush a leaf. True garlic chives smell of garlic. Any grass-like leaf that doesn't is not food.
name: Chinese Chive
preparation: Eat fresh or cooked. The unopened flower buds are the best part.

uses.note: leaves and buds, fresh or cooked

codex: The little heart-pods give it away. A weed of every continent that followed humans here and stayed for dinner.
description: a low rosette with tiny heart-shaped seed pods on wiry stems

knowledgeLevels.1: Shepherd's purse. Tiny heart-shaped pods on wiry stems.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young rosette leaves and the peppery seed pods. A classic spring green.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: soup, dumplings, porridge herb. Vitamin C when you need it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: gather rosettes before the stem bolts. The pods dry for a peppery seasoning. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: The heart-shaped (triangular) seed pods are unmistakable — no lookalike carries them. Rosette leaves are best before the stem shoots up.
name: Shepherd's Purse
preparation: Eat young leaves raw or cooked; the seed pods are peppery. A safe beginner green.

uses.note: young leaves; peppery pods

codex: Red lanterns on a thorny shrub. The birds strip them by fall's end — pick with them, not after them.
description: a thorny arching shrub hung with small oblong red berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Goji. Small red berries on a thorny shrub.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the ripe berries — soft, sweet-tart. Dry them like raisins.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: trail food, soup, tea. Stores dried for months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shake the branches over a cloth. Dry in the sun until leathery. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Goji grows on a thorny UPRIGHT shrub. Bittersweet nightshade makes similar red berries but on a CLIMBING vine with purple star flowers — that one is poison. Shrub = goji; vine = walk away.
name: Goji Berry
preparation: Eat ripe berries fresh or dried. The thorny shrub is the ID — never pick red berries off a vine.

uses.note: fresh or dried berries

codex: The silkworm tree, feeding whoever's hungry now. Wait for the dark ones — the white ones are a lesson in patience.
description: a fast-growing tree dropping dark purple berries that stain the ground

knowledgeLevels.1: Mulberry. Dark purple berries staining the ground purple.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe berries only — dark, soft, sweet. Unripe white/green ones with milky sap cause nausea.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fresh eating, jam, dried. The leaves feed silkworms — a trade good if anyone's raising them.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: spread a cloth and shake. The ripe ones fall; the unripe ones cling. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Only the dark, soft, sweet berries are food. White or green berries with milky sap will turn your stomach — patience is the whole technique.
name: White Mulberry
preparation: Eat ripe (dark, soft) berries fresh or dried. Avoid unripe white/green fruit.

uses.note: ripe berries fresh, dried, or jam

codex: Spring fruit on an evergreen tree — the loquat fruits while everything else is still waking up. Sweet flesh, treacherous seeds.
description: an evergreen tree with big veined leaves and clusters of yellow-orange fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Loquat. Yellow-orange fruit in clusters on an evergreen tree.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the flesh only. The big brown seeds carry amygdalin — spit them out, don't chew them.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: spring fruit when little else is ripe. Jam, poached, fresh.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick fully yellow-soft. The seeds are large — teach everyone to spit. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: The flesh is safe and sweet; the SEEDS are the danger (cyanide compounds if chewed). Eat the fruit, spit the seeds — every time.
name: Loquat
preparation: Eat the ripe flesh fresh or as jam. Always spit out the seeds — they contain amygdalin.

uses.note: fresh flesh; jam (seeds discarded)

codex: Square stem, serrated leaf, unmistakable smell. The mint family's loud cousin — crush it and there's no doubt.
description: a bushy herb with serrated purple-green leaves on square stems

knowledgeLevels.1: Perilla. Serrated leaves, square stems, strong smell when crushed.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the leaves — the smell is the ID. Wraps, pickles, seasoning.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fresh wraps for anything rich; dried and salted for winter.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pinch the tops to bush it out. It self-seeds — let one plant go and you'll never plant again. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Crush the leaf: true perilla smells sharp and unmistakable, and the stem is square (mint family). No smell + round stem = not perilla.
name: Perilla (Shiso)
preparation: Eat fresh as wraps or pickled. The smell test is the ID.

uses.note: fresh leaves; pickled

codex: Tong ho — the chrysanthemum you eat. Floral, green, a little wild; the hot-pot herb that grows itself.
description: a feathery-leaved herb with daisy-like buds, smelling faintly floral

knowledgeLevels.1: Edible chrysanthemum. Feathery leaves, faint floral smell.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves and stems. A classic hot-pot green.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: quick-cooked greens, soup herb. Cut and it regrows.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest before buds open for the tenderest leaves. Succession-sow the patch. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Edible chrysanthemum smells faintly floral-sweet when crushed, and the leaves are deeply cut and feathery. Ornamental mums smell sharp-medicinal — eat only the sweet-smelling one.
name: Chrysanthemum Greens
preparation: Cook the young leaves briefly — hot-pot style. Best before flowering.

uses.note: quick-cooked greens

codex: The field weed that never left. Peppery greens in spring, sharp seeds in fall — the mustard that feeds twice.
description: a weedy mustard with yellow flowers and peppery basal leaves

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild mustard. Yellow flowers, peppery leaves.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves (peppery greens), unopened buds (like tiny broccoli), seeds (mustard).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: spring greens, potherb, seed mustard. A famine food with dignity.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: graze the rosettes before flowering. Save seed heads for seasoning. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Four-petaled yellow flowers and peppery bite = mustard family, safe. The basal rosette is the eating stage; once it bolts tall and tough, take the buds instead.
name: Field Mustard
preparation: Eat young leaves and buds raw or cooked; grind ripe seeds for mustard.

uses.note: leaves, buds, seeds

codex: Golden needles — the dried buds chefs pay for. Fresh ones ask for the pot; a few stomachs ask for caution first.
description: tawny trumpet flowers on arching stems, buds like golden needles

knowledgeLevels.1: Daylily. Tawny trumpet flowers, long buds.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: unopened buds (golden needles) — cook them. Some people react to daylily; try a little first.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: buds in soup and stir-fry; dried buds are the prized golden needles.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick buds the day before they'd open. Dry on racks for the winter store. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: True daylily (Hemerocallis) has fibrous roots, not bulbs — if it grows from a true bulb, it's a true lily and may be toxic. Fibrous roots + tawny trumpets = daylily.
name: Daylily Bud
preparation: Cook the unopened buds; dry for golden needles. Try a small portion first — a few people react.

uses.note: cooked buds; dried golden needles

codex: Fish mint. It smells like a tidepool and tastes like one too — an acquired love, and a free salad.
description: heart-shaped leaves in wet ground smelling faintly of fish when crushed

knowledgeLevels.1: Fish mint. Heart-shaped leaves in the wet ground, fishy smell.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves and tender stems. The fishy smell is the ID — nothing else smells like it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fresh salad herb, cold dishes, soup garnish. Loves wet feet.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it spreads by runners — contain it or feed the village with it. Pick the tender tops. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Crush it: the fishy smell is unmistakable and no lookalike has it. Heart-shaped leaves + wet ground + fish smell = fish mint.
name: Fish Mint
preparation: Eat fresh in salads and cold dishes. The smell cooks off but the crunch stays.

uses.note: fresh herb; soup garnish

codex: The queen of poisons wears a mountain-green disguise. Every spring someone mistakes her for dinner. Be the someone who doesn't.
description: tall spikes of helmet-shaped purple-blue flowers; young shoots like asparagus

knowledgeLevels.1: Aconite. Helmet-shaped purple-blue flowers on tall spikes.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON: every part carries aconitine — roots, shoots, leaves, flowers. Cooking does NOT detoxify. A few grams can stop a heart.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. It is medicine only in expert hands after elaborate processing, and never yours. Mark every patch.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: learn it so you never pick it. The young shoots mimic edible mountain greens — that mimicry kills. Teach the village the helmet flower.

lookalikeNote: THE KILLER MISTAKE: young aconite shoots look like edible spring mountain greens. Rule: never gather an unidentified spring shoot. The helmet-shaped flower is the giveaway — by then it's too late for whoever picked the shoot.
name: Aconite (Monkshood)
preparation: DO NOT EAT. All parts contain aconitine; cooking does not detoxify. Symptoms: tingling mouth, vomiting, heart arrhythmia — can kill within hours.
sources: FDA Talk Paper T01-19 — Aconitum carmichaelii

codex: The trumpet flower that lies. Its seedlings pass for potherbs — in Guizhou, one bowl of mistaken seedlings killed a family.
description: rank-smelling weed with white trumpet flowers and spiny seed pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Jimsonweed. White trumpet flowers, spiny pods, rank smell.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON: tropane alkaloids — hallucinations, racing heart, death. The SEEDLINGS look like edible greens; that mistake has killed families.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. Not medicine, not food, not worth a second look. Pull it with gloves if it invades the garden.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: teach the seedlings to everyone — toothed oval leaves, rank smell when crushed. If a 'wild vegetable' smells rank and wrong, it is.

lookalikeNote: The seedlings are the trap: gathered as wild greens in China with fatal results (documented Guizhou family poisoning). Mature plant is obvious — trumpet flowers, spiny pods, foul smell. Learn the seedling, not the flower.
name: Jimsonweed
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Tropane alkaloids cause delirium, rapid heartbeat, and death. Seedlings have been fatally mistaken for edible greens.
sources: BMC Pharmacology and Toxicology — Guizhou Datura case

codex: The parsnip that isn't. White roots, yellow sap, a smell like the vegetable drawer — and enough cicutoxin in one bite to end you.
description: white umbrella flowers over hollow purple-streaked stems in the marsh

knowledgeLevels.1: Water hemlock. White umbrella flowers, hollow stems, marsh ground.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON: the white tuberous roots look like wild parsnip. One bite can kill — cicutoxin, seizures, no antidote.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. Cut the stem and yellow oily sap oozes out, smelling of parsnip — that's the warning.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the stem base is swollen, the leaf veins end in the notches (not the tips) — unique in the family. Teach it; the marsh is full of it.

lookalikeNote: Mistaken for wild parsnip: white clustered roots, parsnip smell. Tell it by the swollen stem base and the yellow oily sap from a cut stem. Water parsnip lacks both. When in doubt in the marsh, eat nothing root-shaped.
name: Water Hemlock
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Cicutoxin causes seizures and respiratory paralysis; a 2-3cm piece of root can be fatal. No antidote.
sources: CDC MMWR — Water Hemlock Poisoning, Maine 1992

codex: The vine that apes the goji. Red berries, purple stars — pretty, climbing, and full of solanine.
description: a scrambling vine with purple star flowers maturing to red oval berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Bittersweet nightshade. Purple star flowers, red berries, climbing vine.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON: solanine in the berries — nausea, vomiting, worse in quantity. The berries ape goji at a glance.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. The vine climbs; the shrub stands — that's the whole distinction.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: drill the village: goji grows on a thorny UPRIGHT shrub; nightshade CLIMBS with purple flowers. Never pick red berries off a vine.

lookalikeNote: Goji's red berries grow on a thorny upright SHRUB. Nightshade's grow on a CLIMBING vine with purple star-shaped flowers. Shrub = goji; vine = poison. This is the pair that tests whether you learned the goji lesson.
name: Bittersweet Nightshade
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Berries contain solanine — gastrointestinal poisoning. Easily confused with goji at a glance; check the growth habit.

codex: Crisp white corms under the mud — the water chestnut doesn't taste like much until you need crunch more than flavor.
description: spiky grass tufts in the shallows hiding crisp round corms

knowledgeLevels.1: Water chestnut. Spiky grass in the shallows.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the round corms in the mud. Peel, and always cook — ditch water carries flukes.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: crunch that survives cooking — stir-fry, soup, ground for flour.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: rake the mud in fall when the tops brown. Keep peeled corms in clean water. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: True water chestnut is a sedge — spiky grass-like tufts, round crisp corms. Don't confuse with ornamental water plants; if the corm isn't crisp-white inside, don't eat it.
name: Water Chestnut
preparation: Dig the corms, peel, and boil or stir-fry. Always cook — paddy and ditch water can carry parasites.

uses.note: cooked corms; flour

codex: Spring's first vegetable. The shoot is a promise the whole grove keeps — peel it, boil it, and it feeds you like grain.
description: a pale pointed shoot pushing up through leaf litter

knowledgeLevels.1: Bamboo shoot. Pale, pointed, pushing out of the ground near the poles.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the tender shoot (peel the sheaths, eat the core). Raw shoots carry taxiphyllin — a cyanide compound. Boiling destroys it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: boil 20-30 minutes and discard the water. Slice thin for soup, chunk for stew. A spring staple — harvest daily while they come.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: take shoots under 30cm, snap-clean at the base. Boil with the lid off. 2x yield from a good brake.

lookalikeNote: Only take shoots you watched emerge from a food bamboo. Ornamental bamboos run far more bitter and toxic — if you didn't see it planted as food, leave it.
name: Bamboo Shoot
preparation: Peel the tough sheaths, slice, and boil 20-30 minutes; discard the water. Never eat raw.
sources: National Geographic — bamboo shoots superfood piece

uses.note: boiled shoots; soup and stew vegetable

codex: Apple-crisp fresh, date-sweet dried. The tree fruits whether or not anyone is watching — plant once, eat for a lifetime.
description: a small thorny tree with wrinkled reddish-brown fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Jujube. Small tree, wrinkled red-brown fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the fruit — crisp like apple when fresh, sweet like dates dried.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fresh eating, dried for winter, boiled into tonic soups.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest at full red-brown. Dry on the branch or in the sun. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Ripe jujubes are deep red-brown and wrinkled like big dates. Unripe ones are green-yellow and bland — wait for the wrinkle.
name: Jujube
preparation: Eat fresh when crisp; dry for winter stores. The wrinkled red fruit is ripe.

uses.note: fresh or dried fruit
